answer:
ANSWERS (NOAA CO-OPS, as stated on tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov, retrieved 2026-11-24)

1) Current basis for official U.S. tidal datums — the 1983-2001 National Tidal Datum Epoch (the fourth NTDE, 19 years).
   Verbatim: "The present NTDE is 1983 through 2001 and is actively considered for revision every 20-25 years." (https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum_options.html, sha256 b8c630b36f09)
   Corroborating: "NOAA currently utilizes the 1983-2001 National Tidal Datum Epoch. This epoch is now undergoing revision and will be replaced by the fifth iteration of the NTDE." (https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/, sha256 4fa508e48279)
   Corroborating: "The 'Present Epoch' is from 1983-2001 and is the latest bench mark sheet available. The 'Superseded Epoch' is from 1960-1978..." (https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/products.html, sha256 a91d7c87a131)

2) Water-level data years for the replacement (fifth) NTDE — 2002-2020 (19 years).
   Verbatim: "Measurements for the update will be based on water level data spanning the years 2002-2020." (https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/, sha256 4fa508e48279)
   Corroborating: "...except for the 130 19-year control stations. These stations will have collected 19 years of 2002-2020 data at the end of calendar year 2020." and "The 2002-2020 NTDE has been adopted to ensure that all tidal datums throughout the United States are based on one specific common reference period." (https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/faq.html, sha256 27ea305a13c5)

3) Currently proposed release year for products based on the new epoch — 2029.
   Verbatim: "The current proposed release date for new NTDE products is in 2029." (https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/, sha256 4fa508e48279)
   Corroborating: "The NTDE update will be considered complete once all currently published datums and BM sheets (~2,000 stations) have been re-processed. CO-OPS is currently scheduled to complete this work in 2029. We will communicate progress on a periodic basis and any changes to the schedule as necessary." (https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/faq.html, sha256 27ea305a13c5)

SUMMARY TABLE
  Ask | Item | Answer | Source page
  2   | Current NTDE in force | 1983-2001 (fourth epoch, 19 yr) | datum_options.html; datum-updates/ntde/; products.html
  3   | Fifth-epoch data window | 2002-2020 (19 yr) | datum-updates/ntde/; datum-updates/ntde/faq.html
  4   | Proposed release year for new-epoch products | 2029 | datum-updates/ntde/; datum-updates/ntde/faq.html

NOTES ON SCOPE, CURRENCY, AND EVIDENCE
- Ask 1 in the request is a framing constraint ("According to NOAA CO-OPS, ..."), not a value ask, so it carries no numeric result.
- The harness's proofs of absence are page-scoped and are not proofs about the grounding as a whole. They show only that (a) the fifth-epoch data window is not mentioned on datum_options.html, and (b) release timing is not mentioned on datum_options.html, /datum-updates/, or /products.html. Both facts are stated explicitly on /datum-updates/ntde/ and /datum-updates/ntde/faq.html, so neither ask is reported as not stated; the conditional trigger ("if the answer ... is that the page states none") is not met.
- The absence of the strings "2026-2045" and "2030" from those pages is consistent with the grounded values: NOAA's fifth epoch is 2002-2020, and the proposed release is 2029. No 2026-2045 window or 2030 release year appears anywhere in the retrieved CO-OPS text.
- Status wording matters for interpretation: 1983-2001 is the epoch *in force* ("currently utilizes", "present NTDE"); 2002-2020 is *adopted for the replacement* but its products are not yet released; 2029 is expressly a *proposed/current proposed* date and CO-OPS states it will announce schedule changes. Treat 2029 as provisional, not committed.
- Exceptions: "Tidal datums in certain regions with anomalous sea level changes (Alaska, U.S. Gulf Coast) are calculated on a Modified 5-Year Epoch" (datum_options.html) — the 19-year NTDE is the national default, not universal.
- Why it matters: the NTDE defines the reference for MLLW, MHW, MSL and related datums used in tide predictions, bench mark sheets, and nautical chart vertical references; an epoch change shifts published datum values at essentially every station (~2,000 stations to be re-processed per the FAQ).
- Citation basis: quotations are from the pages as fetched 2026-11-24T02:10:17Z-02:10:18Z with the sha256 prefixes listed above; CO-OPS states its schedule may change, so re-verify the NTDE landing page before relying on 2029 in a published document.

question: X38
shape: Traffic signals, FHWA MUTCD (11th Edition vs 2009)
answer:
MUTCD SECTION 4I.06 — PEDESTRIAN INTERVALS AND SIGNAL PHASES: THREE-VALUE LOOKUP

ANSWERS (11th Edition, December 2023, unless labeled otherwise)

1. Minimum buffer interval (steady UPRAISED HAND) before release of a conflicting vehicular movement: 2 SECONDS. Standard, Section 4I.06 Paragraph 4.
2. Default walking speed for sizing pedestrian clearance time: 3.5 FEET PER SECOND. Guidance, Section 4I.06 Paragraph 10 (unchanged from the 2009 Edition).
3. Buffer-interval minimum in the 2009 MUTCD: 3 SECONDS. Standard, Section 4E.06 Paragraph 4 (Figure 4E-2: '3 seconds MIN.').

So the 11th Edition REDUCED the buffer-interval minimum from 3 s to 2 s. This is the single most consequential change among the three values and the one most likely to be misapplied from memory or from a 2009-era timing sheet.

---

SOURCE TEXT (verbatim, as fetched)

11th Edition, Section 4I.06, Paragraph 4 (Standard):
"A pedestrian change interval consisting of a flashing UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall begin immediately following the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication. Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement. The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time (see Paragraphs 7 through 16 of this Section). The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used."

11th Edition, Figure 4I-4 note:
"*** The Buffer Interval, which shall always be provided and displayed, may be used to help satisfy the calculated pedestrian clearance time, or may begin after the calculated pedestrian clearance time has ended."

11th Edition, Section 4I.06, Paragraph 10 (Guidance):
"Where pedestrians who walk slower than 3.5 feet per second, or pedestrians who use wheelchairs, routinely use the crosswalk, a walking speed of less than 3.5 feet per second should be considered in determining the pedestrian clearance time."

2009 MUTCD, Section 4E.06, Paragraph 4 (Standard):
"...Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 3 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement. The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time..."

2009 MUTCD, Figure 4E-2 (long description): "A buffer interval of 3 second MIN. during a steady upraised hand display."

2009 MUTCD, Section 4E.06 (Guidance): "...the pedestrian clearance time should be sufficient to allow a pedestrian crossing in the crosswalk who left the curb or shoulder at the end of the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication to travel at a walking speed of 3.5 feet per second to at least the far side of the traveled way or to a median of sufficient width for pedestrians to wait."

---

EDITION COMPARISON TABLE

| Parameter | 2009 MUTCD | 11th Ed. (Dec 2023) | Provision type |
|---|---|---|---|
| Buffer interval minimum (steady HAND before conflicting release) | 3 s (Sec. 4E.06 ¶4) | 2 s (Sec. 4I.06 ¶4) | Standard ('shall') in both |
| Default pedestrian walking speed | 3.5 ft/s (Sec. 4E.06 Guidance) | 3.5 ft/s (Sec. 4I.06 ¶10 Guidance) | Guidance ('should') in both — unchanged |
| Sum of pedestrian change interval + buffer vs. clearance time | sum >= clearance time | sum >= clearance time | Standard, unchanged |
| Buffer start vs. red clearance | not later than start of red clearance, if used | not later than start of red clearance, if used | Standard, unchanged |
| Buffer always displayed | yes (Fig. 4E-2 note) | yes (Fig. 4I-4 note) | Standard |

---

HOW THE THREE VALUES INTERLOCK (design application)

- The 2 s is a floor, not a target. It is the minimum steady-HAND time that must elapse between the end of the flashing HAND and the instant a conflicting movement (typically a permissive left turn or the cross-street green) is released. A timings sheet showing 0 s or 1 s of steady HAND before a conflicting release is non-compliant under the 11th Edition, and was already non-compliant under the 2009 Edition.
- The buffer is counted inside, not on top of, the pedestrian clearance time. Per the Figure 4I-4 note, the buffer may be used to help satisfy the calculated clearance time. So the flashing HAND is shortened by the buffer length, not extended by it.
- Walking speed is the divisor that sets the clearance time: clearance time = crossing distance / walking speed. 3.5 ft/s is the default; it is a Guidance value, so a lower speed (commonly 3.0 ft/s, or lower for a known slow-pedestrian population, school crossing, or high wheelchair volume) is an engineering-judgment deviation that must be documented, per ¶10.
- Countdown interaction: the countdown terminates at the end of the pedestrian change interval (¶6), so the buffer is displayed after the countdown reaches zero and the display goes dark. The 2 s buffer is therefore invisible to the countdown and must be accounted for separately in the controller timing.

WORKED CHECK (illustrative; confirms the stated bounds are mutually satisfiable)

Crossing: 60 ft, curb to far curb, no median. Default speed 3.5 ft/s.
  Pedestrian clearance time = 60 / 3.5 = 17.1 s.
  Allocate buffer = 2.0 s (meets the 2 s minimum, 11th Ed.).
  Flashing HAND (pedestrian change interval) = 17.1 - 2.0 = 15.1 s.
  Check: 15.1 + 2.0 = 17.1 s >= 17.1 s required. Passes.
  Check: buffer 2.0 s >= 2.0 s minimum. Passes.
  Check: buffer begins at the end of the flashing HAND, which is not later than the start of the red clearance interval if one is used. Passes, provided the controller places the buffer at or before red-clearance onset.
  Same crossing under the 2009 Edition: buffer 3.0 s, flashing HAND 14.1 s, sum still 17.1 s. Note the 2009 rule would have required one additional second of steady HAND and one fewer second of flashing HAND for identical geometry.

---

SCOPE AND CAVEATS

- These are lookups against the published standards, not design recommendations. No engineering judgment is exercised in the three values themselves.
- Provision type matters for enforcement: the 2 s buffer (11th Ed.) and 3 s buffer (2009) are Standards — mandatory. The 3.5 ft/s walking speed is Guidance — a default that may be reduced with justification.
- 2009 Edition revision status: the 3 s value is confirmed in both the original 2009 Edition text and the 2009 Revisions 1&2 consolidated Part 4 PDF. Revision 3 (May 2012) was not separately retrieved; no change to Section 4E.06 ¶4 in that revision is known, so the 3 s answer stands as the 2009 MUTCD value.
- 11th Edition errata: the 2 s value is taken from the FHWA-published 11th Edition Part 4 PDF as released December 2023. No later errata affecting Section 4I.06 ¶4 are known to this lookup.
- Section 4I.06 contains additional pedestrian-interval provisions (walk interval 7 s Guidance / 4 s Option, leading pedestrian interval 3 s Guidance, countdown display rules) that are outside the three asks and are not restated as answers here.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 2 on highways.dot.gov/media/111811 and 3 on mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/htm/2009/part4/part4e.htm. The first reads: "Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement."

question: X39
shape: Oil spill prevention, US EPA (SPCC applicability)
answer:
# SPCC Applicability: The Two Capacity Ceilings and the Aboveground Counting Rule

## 1. Answer in brief

A non-transportation-related onshore facility storing oil is **outside** the coverage of EPA's Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasure (SPCC) rule, 40 CFR Part 112, on capacity grounds only if it stays at or under **both** of these ceilings:

| # | Ceiling (aggregate, facility-wide) | Value | Test applied by EPA | Status at exactly the ceiling |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Aggregate **aboveground** oil storage capacity | **1,320 US gallons** | "Is the total aggregate capacity of aboveground oil storage containers **greater than** 1,320 gallons of oil?" | At exactly 1,320 gal the facility is **not** covered on this basis |
| 2 | Aggregate **completely buried** tank oil storage capacity | **42,000 US gallons** | "Is the total aggregate capacity of completely buried storage tanks **greater than** 42,000 gallons of oil?" | At exactly 42,000 gal the facility is **not** covered on this basis |

The two tests are **disjunctive for coverage and conjunctive for exemption**: exceeding *either* ceiling brings the facility into coverage; staying at or under *both* is required to remain outside. So the governing statement is:

> Exempt on capacity grounds  ⇔  (AG ≤ 1,320 gal) **AND** (BURIED ≤ 42,000 gal)

where AG is the aggregate aboveground capacity computed under §2 below and BURIED is the aggregate capacity of completely buried tanks as defined in 40 CFR 112.2.

Both ceilings are expressed in **US gallons** and are compared against **shell capacity**, not working volume or typical inventory: "Storage capacity of a container means the shell capacity of the container" (40 CFR 112.2). A container counts at its full shell capacity whether it is full, partly full, or empty-but-not-permanently-closed.

## 2. Which aboveground containers count toward the 1,320-gallon total

### 2.1 Inclusions
Count the shell capacity of every container that meets **all** of the following:

1. **It is a container that holds (or is intended to hold) oil.** "Oil" under Part 112 means oil of any kind and in any form — petroleum oils (gasoline, diesel, lube oil, hydraulic oil, fuel oil, used oil) and non-petroleum oils (vegetable oil, animal fat, other non-petroleum oils), per 40 CFR 112.2. Capacity is aggregated regardless of oil type.
2. **Its capacity is 55 US gallons or greater.** The rule states: "For the purposes of this exemption, only containers with a capacity of 55 U.S. gallons or greater are counted" (40 CFR 112.1(d)(1)(ii)). A nominal 55-gallon drum counts; anything smaller does not. Note the parallel exemption for "Any container with a storage capacity of less than 55 gallons of oil" (40 CFR 112.1(d)(5)).
3. **It is aboveground, partially buried, bunkered, or in a vault.** 40 CFR 112.1(b) provides that the term "facility" includes:
   - "(1) Any aboveground container;
   - (2) Any completely buried tank as defined in § 112.2;
   - (3) Any container that is used for standby storage, for seasonal storage, or for temporary storage, or not otherwise 'permanently closed' as defined in § 112.2;
   - (4) Any 'bunkered tank' or 'partially buried tank' as defined in § 112.2, or any container in a vault, **each of which is considered an aboveground storage container for purposes of this part**."

   The practical consequence of (b)(4): partially buried tanks, bunkered tanks and containers inside vaults are **counted in the aboveground total**, not the buried total. The practical consequence of (b)(3): idle, standby, seasonal, temporary, and empty-but-not-permanently-closed containers count at full shell capacity. Only a container that is **permanently closed as defined in 112.2** drops out.

In practice this means: fixed ASTs; shop-fabricated and field-erected tanks; drums and barrels of 55 gal or more; intermediate bulk containers (totes) of 55 gal or more; mobile/portable tanks and skid tanks; cargo tanks, trailer-mounted tanks, and pickup/truck-bed tanks that are used on the site (EPA's SPCC FAQ for farms states expressly: "you should include fuel tanks mounted on trailers, fuel trucks used exclusively on the farm and tanks in pickups toward the overall threshold of 1,320 gallons. Also, count 55-gallon drums, but don't count any container smaller than that."); bunkered and partially buried tanks; and containers in vaults.

### 2.2 Exclusions (do not count toward the aboveground total)
The aboveground aggregate "excludes" the following, per 40 CFR 112.1(d)(1)(ii)(A)-(F):

- (A) the capacity of a container that is **"permanently closed"** as defined in 112.2;
- (B) the capacity of a **"motive power container"** as defined in 112.2 (an onboard container supplying oil consumed by the engine that powers the vehicle, vessel or equipment itself — this does **not** cover a cargo/trailer/drop tank that merely rides on a vehicle);
- (C) the capacity of **hot-mix asphalt** or any hot-mix asphalt container;
- (D) the capacity of a container for **heating oil used solely at a single-family residence**;
- (E) the capacity of **pesticide application equipment and related mix containers**;
- (F) the capacity of any **milk and milk product container** and associated piping and appurtenances.

Also excluded, by separate provisions of 112.1(d):
- any container with a storage capacity of **less than 55 gallons** of oil (112.1(d)(5));
- any facility or part thereof **used exclusively for wastewater treatment** and not used to satisfy any requirement of Part 112 (112.1(d)(6)) — note that "the production, recovery, or recycling of oil is not wastewater treatment for purposes of this paragraph";
- **motive power containers** (112.1(d)(7)); hot-mix asphalt (112.1(d)(8)); single-family residential heating oil (112.1(d)(9)); pesticide application equipment (112.1(d)(10));
- **intra-facility gathering lines** subject to 49 CFR part 192 or 195 (112.1(d)(11)) — flow lines are not containers in any case.

### 2.3 Containers that never count in either total
- **Completely buried tanks** are not part of the aboveground total. They are counted only in the 42,000-gallon buried-tank total. (For the buried total, EPA's applicability screen further directs that you "[d]o not include completely buried tanks subject to all technical requirements of 40 CFR 280/281, containers less than 55 gallons, permanently closed containers, or storage containers used exclusively for wastewater treatment.")
- Containers that never hold oil (e.g., water, brine, air, inert gas, dry product) do not count. Containers that hold oil only incidentally as residue should be evaluated individually; if the container's use is oil storage, it counts.

## 3. The buried-tank total (for completeness, since it gates the same determination)

BURIED = sum of shell capacities of **completely buried tanks** as defined in 40 CFR 112.2, excluding (i) completely buried tanks subject to all technical requirements of 40 CFR parts 280/281, (ii) containers under 55 gallons, (iii) permanently closed containers, and (iv) containers used exclusively for wastewater treatment. Partially buried and bunkered tanks are **not** buried tanks for this purpose — 112.1(b)(4) makes them aboveground storage containers.

## 4. Step-by-step determination procedure

**Step 1 — Fix the facility boundary.** Aggregate all oil storage within the single SPCC "facility" (the onshore building/property/parcel/lease/structure/installation/equipment/pipe/pipeline used in oil storage, transfer, distribution, use, etc., per 112.2). Capacity is aggregated facility-wide; how containers are distributed across the site does not change the totals. Do not split a single facility to stay under a ceiling.

**Step 2 — Inventory every container.** Walk the site and record: container ID, type (AST, drum, tote, skid tank, trailer/pickup tank, partially buried, bunkered, vaulted, completely buried), **shell capacity in US gallons**, contents (oil vs non-oil), current status (in service, standby, seasonal, temporary, empty, permanently closed), and the regulatory basis for any exclusion.

**Step 3 — Compute AG.** AG = Σ shell capacity of all containers meeting §2.1 above. Exclude per §2.2 and §2.3. Do not net out secondary containment, dikes, or freeboard; do not use working volume.

**Step 4 — Compute BURIED.** BURIED = Σ shell capacity of completely buried tanks per §3.

**Step 5 — Apply the two ceilings.**
- If AG > 1,320 gal → the facility is covered by Part 112 on capacity grounds. Stop; the buried total is irrelevant to coverage (though it is still needed for the Plan).
- If AG ≤ 1,320 gal → check BURIED. If BURIED > 42,000 gal → covered. If BURIED ≤ 42,000 gal → **outside** coverage on capacity grounds.

**Step 6 — Do not stop at capacity.** Being under both ceilings is necessary but not sufficient for "outside the rule"; the facility must also fail the other applicability elements. EPA's screen asks, in order: (1) Is the facility or part of it non-transportation-related? (2) Is it engaged in drilling, producing, gathering, storing, processing, refining, transferring, distributing, using or consuming oil? (3) Could it reasonably be expected to discharge oil in quantities that may be harmful into navigable waters or adjoining shorelines? Only then do the 1,320 / 42,000 capacity questions apply. A facility that is under both ceilings but otherwise meets the tests is still outside on capacity grounds; a facility over a ceiling is in.

**Step 7 — Document the determination.** Keep a dated capacity determination in the facility's files (or in the SPCC Plan if one exists): the container inventory, shell capacities, the exclusion claimed for each excluded container with its regulatory cite (e.g., "112.1(d)(1)(ii)(B) motive power container — onboard tank of forklift #3"), the AG and BURIED totals, and the resulting conclusion. Re-run the determination whenever a container is added, removed, permanently closed, or converted to oil service.

### Worksheet template

| Container ID | Type | Shell cap. (US gal) | Oil? (Y/N) | Counts in AG? | Counts in BURIED? | Exclusion cite |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T-101 | Vertical AST | 12,000 | Y | Y | N | — |
| D-01…D-40 | 55-gal drums | 55 each | Y | Y (55 ≥ 55) | N | — |
| D-41 | 30-gal drum | 30 | Y | N | N | 112.1(d)(5) (<55 gal) |
| T-102 | Tank, permanently closed | 500 | Y | N | N | 112.1(d)(1)(ii)(A) |
| T-103 | Partially buried tank | 1,000 | Y | Y | N | 112.1(b)(4) — aboveground |
| U-01, U-02 | Completely buried tanks | 10,000 each | Y | N | Y | — |

AG = Σ (Counts in AG? = Y); BURIED = Σ (Counts in BURIED? = Y).

## 5. Worked examples (arithmetic shown, boundary cases included)

**Example A — covered via the aboveground ceiling.** 12,000-gal AST + 8,000-gal AST + 40 drums × 55 gal (= 2,200 gal) + a 300-gal tank mounted on a service truck used on site. A 30-gal drum is excluded (<55 gal); a 500-gal permanently closed tank is excluded. AG = 12,000 + 8,000 + 2,200 + 300 = **22,500 gal** > 1,320 → **covered**, irrespective of the buried total (here 2 × 10,000 = 20,000 gal, which is under 42,000 but does not rescue the facility).

**Example B — outside on both ceilings (boundary case).** 20 drums × 55 gal = 1,100 gal plus one 220-gal tank = **AG = 1,320 gal exactly** → not greater than 1,320 → passes the aboveground test. One completely buried 40,000-gal tank → **BURIED = 40,000 gal** ≤ 42,000 → passes the buried test. Result: **outside** Part 112 coverage on capacity grounds (subject to the Step 6 checks).

**Example C — outside aboveground but covered via the buried ceiling.** Same aboveground inventory as Example B (AG = 1,320 gal), but two completely buried 25,000-gal tanks → **BURIED = 50,000 gal** > 42,000 → **covered** by Part 112. This is the case most often missed: an operator sees "1,320" satisfied and stops, ignoring buried capacity.

## 6. Common errors this procedure is designed to catch

1. **Counting only 55-gal drums and missing totes, skid tanks, trailer/pickup tanks.** Anything ≥55 gal holding oil counts, including mobile containers.
2. **Dropping a container because it is empty.** Emptiness is not an exclusion; only "permanently closed" (as defined in 112.2) is.
3. **Treating partially buried or bunkered tanks as buried.** 112.1(b)(4) makes them aboveground storage containers.
4. **Counting working volume instead of shell capacity.** Use shell capacity (112.2).
5. **Netting out containment or freeboard.** No netting; the ceiling is on container shell capacity.
6. **Splitting a facility into parcels to stay under a ceiling.** Aggregate facility-wide.
7. **Stopping at 1,320 gal without checking the 42,000-gal buried total** (Example C).
8. **Confusing these applicability ceilings with other Part 112 numbers.** 42,000 gallons *also* appears in Appendix F as the "total oil storage capacity greater than or equal to 42,000 gallons where operations include over-water transfers of oil" substantial-harm criterion for Facility Response Plans, and Appendix F §2.2 uses a 1,000,000-gallon criterion for lack of adequate secondary containment; the 10,000-gallon figure in EPA's guidance is the qualified-facility self-certification tier. None of those is an applicability ceiling — the applicability ceilings are 1,320 gal aboveground and 42,000 gal completely buried.

## 7. Source provenance (so the citation trail is auditable)

- **1,320-gallon aboveground ceiling, the 55-gallon counting cutoff, and the (A)-(F) exclusions** — 40 CFR 112.1(d)(1)(ii), as published at https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/section-112.1 (and mirrored in the 2025 print edition at govinfo.gov, 40 CFR part 112): "The aggregate aboveground storage capacity of the facility is 1,320 U.S. gallons or less of oil. For the purposes of this exemption, only containers with a capacity of 55 U.S. gallons or greater are counted. The aggregate aboveground storage capacity of a facility excludes: (A) … permanently closed … (B) … motive power container … (C) … hot-mix asphalt … (D) … heating oil used solely at a single-family residence; (E) … pesticide application equipment and related mix containers. (F) … milk and milk product container …"
- **What counts as a container (including partially buried, bunkered and vaulted containers as aboveground)** — 40 CFR 112.1(b)(1)-(4).
- **<55-gallon and other container-level exclusions** — 40 CFR 112.1(d)(5)-(12).
- **Shell capacity** — 40 CFR 112.2 ("Storage capacity of a container means the shell capacity of the container").
- **42,000-gallon completely buried tank ceiling and the "greater than" phrasing of both tests** — EPA, "Does the Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasure (SPCC) Rule Apply to Your Facility?" (Questions 4 and 5), https://www.epa.gov/oil-spills-prevention-and-preparedness-regulations/does-spill-prevention-control-and-countermeasure; and EPA SPCC FAQ ("Stores more than 1,320 U.S. gallons in total of all aboveground containers … or more than 42,000 gallons in completely buried containers"), https://www.epa.gov/oil-spills-prevention-and-preparedness-regulations/spill-prevention-control-and-countermeasure-19. The fetched regulatory excerpt of 112.1(d)(1)(ii) does not itself reproduce the buried-tank sentence, so the 42,000-gallon figure is attributed here to EPA's published applicability determination and the Part 112 applicability framework rather than to a specific paragraph number.
- **Note on the not_stated/blocked_on question:** the harness's proof of absence for asks 1 and 3 attaches to https://nepis.epa.gov/Exe/ZyPURL.cgi?Dockey=P100B4Z9.TXT, which resolves to a 48-character document-display stub ("Document Display (PURL) | NSCEP | US EPA") containing no regulatory text at all. That absence is a property of a broken/stub page, not a statement by the rule that no ceiling exists. Both asks are answered verbatim on the eCFR and EPA pages above, so neither ask is listed in not_stated and neither is blocked.

question: X40
shape: Units and conversions, HVAC capacity (NIST SP 811 conversion factors)
answer:
CHILLER CAPACITY CONVERSION — 10 TONS OF REFRIGERATION TO kW

RESULT
  Cooling capacity = 35.17 kW (four significant figures)
  Unrounded: 35.168 53 kW (= 35 168.53 W = 120 000 Btu_IT/h)

1. BASIS AND GOVERNING DEFINITION
The ton of refrigeration is a unit of heat-flow rate (power), not of mass, volume, or water flow. Per NIST SP 811, Appendix B.8 (Factors for Units Listed Alphabetically) and Appendix B.9 (Factors for Units Listed by Kind of Quantity), and NIST SP 1038 Table 5.2.13, the unit is defined as exactly 12 000 Btu_IT per hour, and the official conversion factors published are:

  Source 1 — NIST SP 811, Appendix B.8, alphabetical listing (verbatim):
      "ton of refrigeration (12 000 BtuIT/h)   watt (W)   3.516 853   E+03"
  Source 2 — NIST SP 811, Appendix B.9, "Heat Flow Rate" table (verbatim):
      "ton of refrigeration (12 000 BtuIT/h)   watt (W)   3.516 853   E+03"
  Source 3 — NIST SP 1038, Sec. 5.2.13 "Power" (verbatim):
      "ton, refrigeration (12 000 Btu/h)   kilowatt (kW)   3.516 853"

Adopted factor (the official NIST value, used as published):
      1 ton of refrigeration = 3.516 853 kW = 3 516.853 W

Note on the Btu variant: the NIST entry is explicitly the International Table Btu (Btu_IT), consistent with the request's "12 000 Btu_IT/h". This matters — see Section 5.

2. THE CONVERSION (Ask 2)
      Q [kW] = (tonnage) x (3.516 853 kW/ton)
      Q = 10 ton x 3.516 853 kW/ton
      Q = 35.168 53 kW

Route check A — from the exact Btu_IT definition, quoted verbatim in NIST SP 811: "The Fifth International Conference on the Properties of Steam (London, July 1956) defined the calorie (International Table) as 4.1868 J. Therefore the exact conversion for the Btu (International Table) is 1.055 055 852 62 kJ."
      1 Btu_IT = 1055.055 852 62 J (exact)
      1 ton = 12 000 Btu_IT/h = 12 000 x 1055.055 852 62 J / 3600 s
            = 12 660 670.231 44 / 3600 W
            = 3516.852 842 W = 3.516 852 842 kW  (exact by definition)
      Q = 10 x 3.516 852 842 = 35.168 528 42 kW

Route check B — via the NIST Btu_IT/h-to-watt factor (0.293 071 1 W per Btu_IT/h, SP 811 App. B.9):
      120 000 Btu_IT/h x 0.293 071 1 W/(Btu_IT/h) = 35 168.532 W = 35.168 532 kW

All three routes agree to better than 1 part in 10^6 (the difference is only the rounding in NIST's published 7-figure factor). The published-factor result 35.168 53 kW is the one carried forward, since the request specifies the official published factor.

3. ROUNDING TO FOUR SIGNIFICANT FIGURES (Ask 3)
      35.168 53 kW  ->  digits 3, 5, 1, 7 are the first four significant figures; the fifth digit is 8, so round up:
      = 35.17 kW
  Check: 35.17 has exactly four significant figures (3, 5, 1, 7).
  Not acceptable alternatives: 35.2 kW (three sig figs), 35.168 kW (five sig figs), 35.169 kW (five sig figs).
  Rounding was applied to the final arithmetic result only; the NIST factor itself was used at its published precision (3.516 853), not pre-rounded.

4. EQUIVALENT EXPRESSIONS OF THE SAME CAPACITY (for the equipment schedule / submittal review)
      35.17 kW
      35 168.5 W  (35.168 53 kW unrounded)
      120 000 Btu_IT/h  (= 120 MBH; 120 000/1000 = 120 MBH)
      10 tons of refrigeration (nameplate value)
      35.17 kJ/s
      30.24 ton-hour/h equivalent heat rate is not applicable — no time-integrated energy is implied here.

Reference table, same NIST factor, four significant figures:
      1 ton   = 3.517 kW
      2 ton   = 7.034 kW
      3 ton   = 10.55 kW
      5 ton   = 17.58 kW
      10 ton  = 35.17 kW
      20 ton  = 70.34 kW
      100 ton = 351.7 kW

5. WHAT THIS NUMBER IS AND IS NOT (mechanical scope notes)
  a) Cooling capacity, not electrical input. 35.17 kW is the rate at which the chiller removes heat from the chilled-water loop (gross refrigeration effect). The compressor/motor electrical demand is a separate quantity: P_electrical = Q_cooling / COP (or / EER x 3.412). Example only: at a rated COP of 3.0, input ~11.7 kW; at COP 5.0, ~7.03 kW. Do not put 35.17 kW on an electrical panel schedule as connected load.
  b) Gross vs net capacity. Nameplate tonnage is a nominal gross rating at standard rating conditions (for water-cooled machines typically AHRI 550/590 conditions: 44 deg F leaving chilled water, 95 deg F entering condenser water, 3 gpm/ton evaporator flow, 3 gpm/ton condenser flow). The Btu_IT/h-to-kW conversion itself is exact and condition-independent; the tonnage number is not. Actual capacity at off-design conditions must come from the manufacturer's performance map, and nameplate capacity typically carries a tolerance of about +/-5 percent under AHRI 550/590. No derating, fouling factor, altitude, or net-capacity (minus fan/pump heat) adjustment was requested or applied.
  c) Btu variant sensitivity. If the rating were in Btu_th/h instead (thermochemical, 1 Btu_th = 1054.350 J), the factor would be 0.292 875 1 W per Btu_th/h, i.e. 3.514 501 kW/ton, giving 35.15 kW for 10 tons — a 0.07 percent difference. The NIST definition of the ton of refrigeration uses Btu_IT, and the request specifies Btu_IT, so 35.17 kW is the correct figure. Do not mix the two Btu definitions within one calculation.
  d) Significant-figure caveat for the record. The nameplate input "10 tons" is itself a nominal rating of one or two significant figures; the requested four-significant-figure output (35.17 kW) states the conversion arithmetic precisely, not the physical accuracy of the rating. For submittal or load-calculation use, treat the capacity as ~35.2 kW nominal and confirm against the manufacturer's certified performance data.

6. SUMMARY LINE FOR THE SCHEDULE
      Chiller, nominal cooling capacity: 10 tons refrigeration = 120 000 Btu_IT/h = 35.17 kW (NIST SP 811 factor 3.516 853 kW/ton; exact definitional value 35.168 53 kW).
cautions: The answer gives 35.17 kW for ask 2, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: X41
answer:
ANSWER STATUS

Neither figure requested is stated in Microchip DS40002061B (ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P, Rev. B, 09/2020):

- Ask 2 - junction-to-ambient thermal resistance (degC/W) of the ATmega328P in the 28-lead 0.300in PDIP (Microchip package code 28P3): NOT STATED. The datasheet contains no thermal resistance table, no theta-JA, no theta-JC and no psi-JT values for any of its four packages (28P3 PDIP, 32A TQFP, 28M1 QFN/MLF, 32M1-A VQFN). This is a characteristic of the megaAVR datasheet family: the Electrical Characteristics chapter consists of Absolute Maximum Ratings, DC Characteristics, Speed Grades and System and Device Characteristics, none of which is a thermal characterization section.
- Ask 3 - maximum junction temperature or total power dissipation: NOT STATED. The Absolute Maximum Ratings table gives operating temperature range, storage temperature range, voltage on any pin except RESET, voltage on RESET, DC current per I/O pin, and DC current VCC and GND - it gives no Tj(max) and no Ptot. There is no derating curve and no package power dissipation rating anywhere in the document.

The proof-of-absence searches listed in not_stated cover the secondary pages the harness read in full. The pages of DS40002061B itself that were read in full (513-515 characterization graphs, 483-484, 637-646 package drawings and revision history) likewise carry no thermal data, so nothing in the grounding supplies either number. No figure is given here for either ask.

WHAT THE DATASHEET DOES AND DOES NOT GIVE THE DESIGNER

1. Absolute Maximum Ratings (Electrical Characteristics chapter, the table that begins on the page carrying 'Operating Temperature -55 degC to +125 degC / Storage Temperature -65 degC to +150 degC / Voltage on any Pin except RESET with respect to Ground -0.5 V to VCC+0.5 V / DC Current per I/O Pin 40.0 mA'). These are stress ratings, not operating limits. The 40 mA per-pin figure is a damage threshold, not an operating current.
2. Ordering Information: the ATmega328P in 28P3 is ATmega328P-PU (and ATmega328P-PN for the extended ordering variant), industrial temperature grade -40 degC to +85 degC. That is an ambient/operating temperature grade, NOT a junction temperature; it does not answer ask 3.
3. DC Characteristics: ICC versus VCC and frequency (e.g. the secondary source used here records 5.2 mA typ / 9 mA max at 8 MHz, VCC = 5 V). This is the raw material for a power estimate but is not a dissipation rating.

HOW TO GET A DEFENSIBLE NUMBER (procedure, since the datasheet will not supply one)

Step 1 - Device power. P_device = VCC x ICC(f, VCC, temp) + sum over I/O pins of (IOL x VOL) for sinks and (IOH x (VCC - VOH)) for sources + ADC/peripheral contributions. Use the datasheet's ICC max at the actual operating point, not typical. Worked anchor: 5 V x 9 mA = 45 mW for the core at 8 MHz/5 V worst case. Illustrative I/O load: eight pins sinking 20 mA each at VOL = 0.6 V adds 8 x 0.020 A x 0.6 V = 96 mW, i.e. the I/O can easily exceed the core - this is why the DC current limits, not thermal resistance, govern a 28P3 design in practice.

Step 2 - Rtheta-JA. Obtain it from Microchip, not from another vendor's PDIP. Request the package thermal characterization for 28P3 through a Microchip support ticket or the package thermal data published with the packaging specification (the datasheet itself points to http://www.microchip.com/packaging for current package drawings). Alternatively measure per JEDEC JESD51-2 (still air), JESD51-6 (forced air) and JESD51-8 (junction-to-board), on the actual board copper, with the part soldered (a socket roughly doubles the case-to-ambient path). Report the board, airflow and socket condition with the number - an Rtheta-JA without those conditions is not reusable.

Step 3 - Junction temperature. Tj = Ta + P_device x Rtheta-JA. Because no Tj(max) is published, do not invent one; hold Tj below the reliability limit you can defend from Microchip's qualification data (typically 125 degC for industrial-grade plastic packages, but confirm in writing with Microchip for this device before relying on it), and treat the -40 degC to +85 degC ambient grade as the binding datasheet limit on Ta. Scaling: every 10 degC/W of Rtheta-JA costs 1 degC at 100 mW, so for a 45 mW core the thermal term is small; it only becomes significant when many I/O pins are loaded or when the part sits in a sealed enclosure with elevated internal ambient.

Step 4 - If the application is thermally marginal, the fix is not a datasheet number but a design change: reduce simultaneously-driven I/O current (respect the per-pin 40 mA absolute maximum and derate well below it, e.g. 20 mA continuous), add series resistance or a driver for LEDs, use the TQFP/QFN variants (32A, 28M1) whose exposed/lead-frame area gives a lower Rtheta-JA than a 28P3 in still air, and derate the ambient budget rather than the junction budget.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE REQUESTER

There is no datasheet answer to either question. DS40002061B does not specify Rtheta-JA for the ATmega328P 28P3, and it does not specify a maximum junction temperature or total power dissipation. Any number quoted for these from 'the ATmega328P datasheet' is either from a different document (Microchip package thermal data, JEDEC measurement, an older Atmel package document) or fabricated.
cautions: The answer says ask 2 is not stated in the document. The only check behind that is a search of the pages read in full for the words a model listed as the ones such an answer would be printed with, and it found none.

The answer says ask 3 is not stated in the document. The only check behind that is a search of the pages read in full for the words a model listed as the ones such an answer would be printed with, and it found none.

question: X42
answer:
SOURCE DOCUMENT
Infineon IRF540NPbF datasheet, Rev. 2.1, 2026-07-24 (revision history entry: '2026-07-24 | 2.1 | Update datasheet to Infineon format'). Retrieved copy: https://www.infineon.com/assets/row/public/documents/24/49/infineon-irf540n-datasheet-en.pdf (fetched 2026-11-24T02:25:34Z, sha256 a3fd62a76cc8). The same table text was independently confirmed on two further Infineon-hosted copies of the same revision (sha256 identical): /dgdl/Infineon-IRF540N-DataSheet-v01_01-EN.pdf and /dgdl/irf540npbf.pdf?fileId=5546d462533600a4015355e39f0d19a1.

RELEVANT TABLE TEXT (Absolute Maximum Ratings, page 1, verbatim)
  PD @ TC = 25°C  Maximum Power Dissipation   130   W
  Linear Derating Factor                     0.87  W/°C
  TJ Operating Junction and TSTG Storage Temperature Range  -55 to +175  °C
Thermal Resistance table (same page, verbatim):
  RthJC Junction-to-Case                –––   1.15  °C/W
  Rcs  Case-to-Sink, Flat, Greased Surface  0.50  –––  °C/W

ANSWER 1 — Maximum power dissipation at TC = 25 °C
  PD(25 °C) = 130 W
  This is the absolute-maximum dissipation with the case held at 25 °C, i.e. the reference point of the derating line. It is a package/thermal limit (junction-to-case), not an application rating; it assumes the case is actually held at 25 °C by the external heatsink.

ANSWER 2 — Linear derating factor
  dPD/dTC = 0.87 W/°C
  Reference temperature for the derating is TC = 25 °C (the table row it is attached to is 'PD @ TC = 25°C'), and derating applies for case temperatures above 25 °C, linearly, down to zero at the point where TJ,max is reached.

ANSWER 3 — Maximum power dissipation allowed at TC = 100 °C
  P(100 °C) = PD(25 °C) − (dPD/dTC) × (100 °C − 25 °C)
            = 130 W − 0.87 W/°C × 75 °C
            = 130 W − 65.25 W
            = 64.75 W
  Report as 64.75 W (≈ 64.8 W to 3 s.f.; 65 W if rounded to the 2 s.f. implied by the 0.87 figure).

CROSS-CHECKS (all consistent)
1. Derating factor vs. thermal resistance: 1/RthJC = 1/1.15 °C/W = 0.8696 W/°C → published 0.87 W/°C. The datasheet value is 1/RthJC rounded to two decimals.
2. Zero-dissipation point: 130 W × 1.15 °C/W = 149.5 °C rise; 25 °C + 149.5 °C = 174.5 °C ≈ TJ,max 175 °C. Confirms the derating line is the TJ,max-limited line and that 25 °C is the correct reference.
3. Alternative route at 100 °C: P = (TJ,max − TC)/RthJC = (175 − 100)/1.15 = 65.2 W. This differs from 64.75 W by 0.45 W (0.7%) solely because 0.87 is a rounded reciprocal. The requested linear-derating computation gives 64.75 W; 65.2 W is the thermal-resistance-consistent figure. Use 64.75 W for the stated derating arithmetic and treat ~65 W as the design-margin value.
4. Result is below the 25 °C rating (64.75 W < 130 W) and positive, so it violates no limit stated in this answer; implied TJ at 64.75 W with TC = 100 °C is 100 + 64.75 × 1.15 = 174.5 °C, i.e. at (not above) TJ,max.
5. Secondary consistency: the same table gives ID @ TC = 100 °C = 23 A; 64.75 W / 23 A corresponds to VDS ≈ 2.8 V, i.e. the 100 °C dissipation limit is reachable only in the linear/switching-loss regime — it is a thermal ceiling, not a simultaneous ID × VDS operating point. Also note the Safe Operating Area (Fig. 8) and the transient thermal impedance (Fig. 11) further restrict pulsed operation; the DC derating line is the envelope for continuous operation only.

CAUTIONS FOR THE DOWNSTREAM USER
- Do not source these numbers from the Infineon product landing page (infineon.com/cms/en/product/power/mosfet/n-channel/irf540n/ or the /cms/de/ equivalent). Those pages show 'Ptot max 140 W' and 'RthJC max 1.1 K/W', which disagree with the Rev. 2.1 datasheet (130 W, 1.15 °C/W) and with each other's reciprocal (1/1.1 = 0.91 W/°C ≠ 0.87 W/°C). The datasheet is the controlling document. The harness's proof of absence for ask 2 applies only to those two landing pages (no occurrence of 'Linear derating factor', 'derating factor', 'Linear derating', 'dPtot/dTc', 'dP/D', 'W/°C', 'W/K' in 423,193 characters each); the derating factor is present and explicit in the datasheet PDFs, so ask 2 is answered, not unstated.
- The derating is per °C of CASE temperature, not ambient. In a real design, ambient-referenced derating must add Rth_cs (0.50 °C/W greased flat surface) and the heatsink thermal resistance; the 64.75 W figure is only valid if the heatsink genuinely holds the case at 100 °C.
- Do not use IRFI540NPbF (TO-220 FullPak isolated) figures for this part: that variant's datasheet gives 54 W / 0.36 W/°C. It is a different package and thermal path.
- The 130 W / 0.87 W/°C pair is valid for the cited Rev. 2.1 only; earlier International Rectifier revisions of IRF540N should be re-checked before reuse.
cautions: The answer gives 64.75 W for ask 3, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

# vm.swappiness on a current Linux kernel: range, default, and the value for a 2x-faster swap device

## 1. Basis (ask 1 — the "current Linux kernel" constraint)

All figures below are taken from the current kernel's sysctl documentation, `Documentation/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.html` as served at https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.html (and its `#swappiness` anchor), cross-checked against Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9's memory-tuning guide and the docs.kernel.org 7.1 mirror. That page describes the *current* semantics, including the 0–200 range and the modern meaning of `swappiness = 0`; its header line "valid for Linux kernel version 2.6.29" is an unfixed documentation artifact and is superseded by the body text (the 2x/zram example and the 0–200 range did not exist in 2.6.29). Where a vendor document disagrees (RHEL 10's guide describes the value as a percentage "ranging from 0 to 100"), the kernel's own accepted range governs; vendor docs are a simplification, and distributions may also ship non-upstream defaults (e.g. desktop profiles that lower it to 10–30), which is why the shipped value on a given host must be read, not assumed.

## 2. Accepted range (ask 2)

**`vm.swappiness` accepts integer values in the closed interval 0–200.**

The kernel documentation states it verbatim: "This control is used to define the rough relative IO cost of swapping and filesystem paging, as a value between 0 and 200." The RHEL 9 guide independently states "The swappiness value, ranging from 0 to 200, controls the degree to which the system favors reclaiming memory from the anonymous memory pool, or the page cache memory pool."

Semantics of the scale:
- `100` — the VM assumes swap and filesystem IO cost the same and applies reclaim pressure to page cache and swap-backed pages equally.
- `< 100` — swap IO is treated as more expensive than filesystem paging; anonymous pages are retained longer.
- `> 100` — swap IO is treated as cheaper than filesystem paging; anonymous pages are reclaimed more eagerly. Values above 100 are legal and are specifically recommended for in-memory swap.
- `0` — on a current kernel this is **not** "disable swap": "the kernel will not initiate swap until the amount of free and file-backed pages is less than the high watermark in a zone." Swap can still occur under zone-level pressure. (Vendor docs such as RHEL 9 additionally warn that 0 raises OOM-killer risk under heavy memory/IO pressure.)

## 3. Default (ask 3)

**Default = 60.** Upstream: "The default value is 60." RHEL 9/10 agree. Note that a distribution or a provisioning layer may override this at boot via `sysctl.d`; the effective value is whatever `/proc/sys/vm/swappiness` reads.

## 4. Value for a swap device whose random IO is 2x faster than filesystem IO (ask 4)

**Recommended value: 133.**

This is the kernel documentation's own worked example for exactly this condition, and it falls out of the normalization the scale uses:

- Let the cost of one unit of swap random IO be `x`. Swap is 2x faster, so one unit of filesystem IO costs `2x`.
- The scale spans 200 units across the sum of the two costs: `x + 2x = 3x = 200`.
- The cheap (swap) side consumes `x/3x × 200 = 66.67`; the expensive (filesystem) side consumes `2x/3x × 200 = 133.33`.
- Higher swappiness means swap is relatively cheaper, so the value is the complement of the swap share: `200 − 66.67 = 133.33`, truncated to the integer **133**.

Quote from the source: "For in-memory swap, like zram or zswap, as well as hybrid setups that have swap on faster devices than the filesystem, values beyond 100 can be considered. For example, if the random IO against the swap device is on average 2x faster than IO from the filesystem, swappiness should be 133 (x + 2x = 200, 2x = 133.33)."

Consistency check against the deliverable's own bounds: `0 ≤ 60 ≤ 200` and `0 ≤ 133 ≤ 200`, so both the default and the recommendation are inside the accepted range, and 133's being above 100 is explicitly sanctioned by the same page for in-memory/hybrid swap.

## 5. Why 133, not 260 (reasoning bound)

A naive reading — "swap is 2x faster, so double the default 60 to 120" or "2 × 133 = 266" — is wrong twice over: (a) the scale is a *relative cost* normalization capped at 200, not a linear speed multiplier; (b) the ratio enters as a share of the total cost, so it saturates. A 10x-faster swap device would give `200 − 200/11 ≈ 182`, not 600. Any recommendation must be clamped to 0–200.

## 6. Scope and caveats

- **Global vs per-cgroup.** `vm.swappiness` is the system-wide knob. Cgroup v2 exposes `memory.swappiness` per memory cgroup; a per-cgroup value overrides the global one for reclaim inside that cgroup. If a workload is confined to a memory cgroup, tune both.
- **zram specifics.** zram trades disk IO for CPU compression/decompression and holds data in RAM, so its readback latency is RAM-like and it is effectively much more than 2x faster than filesystem IO on rotating media; the 133 figure is the conservative, documented answer for the stated 2x case. If compression ratio and CPU headroom are healthy, values toward the 150–180 band are defensible — but the documentation is explicit that "An optimal value will require experimentation and will also be workload-dependent," and the 2x premise alone does not justify more than 133.
- **Workload dependence.** Latency-sensitive or anonymous-heavy workloads (databases, VMs, numeric/HPC) do better at lower values; file/streaming workloads benefit from higher values because reclaim then favors retaining page cache. Under sustained pressure, very high swappiness combined with a small zram device causes swap thrash, while very low values push the OOM killer.
- **Related knobs.** `vm.watermark_scale_factor`, `vm.vfs_cache_pressure`, zswap (and its shrinker/limit settings), and zram writeback interact with this choice; do not treat swappiness in isolation.

## 7. Apply and verify procedure

```
# read the effective current values
sysctl vm.swappiness
cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness

# temporary change (takes effect immediately)
sysctl -w vm.swappiness=133
# or: echo 133 > /proc/sys/vm/swappiness

# persistent change
printf 'vm.swappiness = 133\n' > /etc/sysctl.d/90-swappiness.conf
sysctl --system        # or: sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/90-swappiness.conf

# verify
sysctl vm.swappiness     # expect: vm.swappiness = 133

# per-cgroup (cgroup v2), if the workload is in a memory cgroup
echo 133 > /sys/fs/cgroup/<group>/memory.swappiness

# sanity: confirm swap is actually zram and active
swapon --show
zramctl
```

If any write is rejected with `Invalid argument`, the running kernel predates the 0–200 range and only accepts 0–100; then clamp to 100 and re-evaluate the premise (in that case the 2x-faster-swap condition cannot be expressed in the knob at all).

## 8. Final answers

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| 2. accepted range | **0–200** (integers) |
| 3. default | **60** |
| 4. value for a swap device with 2x-faster random IO | **133** |

# multiprocessing default start method on Linux — CPython 3.15 series

Source of record: *multiprocessing — Process-based parallelism*, section "Contexts and start methods", https://docs.python.org/3.15/library/multiprocessing.html (fetched 2026-11-24T02:31:01Z, sha256 1e84b04b3d7e). All quotations below are verbatim from that page. The same text is mirrored on https://docs.python.org/3/library/multiprocessing.html and on the fr/3 translation (same sha256), so the answer does not depend on which of those mirrors is read.

## Answers

### 1. Default on Linux when set_start_method() is never called

**`forkserver`.**

The `forkserver` bullet states:

> "Available on POSIX platforms which support passing file descriptors over Unix pipes such as Linux. **The default on those**, unless there is no writable temporary directory (see `tempfile.gettempdir()`), which the fork server requires; spawn is the default in that case."

> "Changed in version 3.14: This became the default start method on POSIX platforms."

Linux satisfies the stated availability precondition (POSIX plus descriptor passing over Unix pipes), so on Linux the default is `forkserver`, subject only to the exception in ask 3.

The change is corroborated negatively by the `fork` bullet:

> "Changed in version 3.14: This is no longer the default start method on any platform. Code that requires fork must explicitly specify that via `get_context()` or `set_start_method()`."

Two behavioural details that belong with the answer, both from the same page:

- The default is not frozen at import time. Per the 3.15.1 note: "The default is determined when it is first needed rather than when `multiprocessing` is imported."
- `get_start_method(allow_none=True)` returns `None` while the global method is unset; `get_start_method(allow_none=False)` (the default) "will set it to the system default, and its name is returned." `get_context(method=None)` likewise "will set it to the system default." So a program that never calls `set_start_method()` still gets `forkserver` — the default is applied lazily on first need, not skipped.

### 2. Linux default before Python 3.14

**`fork`.**

The "Contexts and start methods" section records the switch explicitly:

> "Changed in version 3.14: On POSIX platforms the default start method was changed from fork to forkserver to retain the performance but avoid common multithreaded process incompatibilities. See gh-84559."

Combined with the 3.14 note in the `fork` bullet ("This is no longer the default start method on any platform"), this fixes `fork` as the pre-3.14 default on Linux for every release from the introduction of start methods (3.4) through 3.13 inclusive. (The macOS exception is separate and older — see the caveat below.)

### 3. Condition under which the default becomes `spawn` instead

**When there is no writable temporary directory** — i.e. when `tempfile.gettempdir()` does not yield a writable location, for example on a read-only file system. `forkserver` requires a writable temp dir for the fork server's Unix socket; if it is unavailable, `spawn` is used instead.

Verbatim:

> "The default on those, unless there is no writable temporary directory (see `tempfile.gettempdir()`), which the fork server requires; **spawn is the default in that case**."

> "Changed in version 3.15.1: spawn is now the default start method when there is no writable temporary directory, for example on a read-only file system. Previously forkserver remained the default there and starting a process failed with an `OSError`. The default is determined when it is first needed rather than when `multiprocessing` is imported. See gh-155717."

This is the *only* Linux condition given on the page for `spawn` becoming the default. On Linux there is no environment-variable or CLI override documented for the start method in this section; `spawn` otherwise becomes the default only via explicit selection (`set_start_method('spawn')`, `get_context('spawn')`, or `-X` style configuration not covered here) or on other platforms (Windows, and macOS since 3.8).

**Version pin:** the spawn-on-no-writable-tempdir behaviour is documented as "Changed in version 3.15.1". On 3.15.0 the second half of that note applied: `forkserver` remained the default and starting a process failed with `OSError`. If the deployment target is exactly 3.15.0, ask 3's condition does not yet hold and the observable outcome is an `OSError` at process start; from 3.15.1 onward it is `spawn`.

## Consolidated answer table

| # | Question | Answer | Authority on the 3.15 page |
|---|----------|--------|----------------------------|
| 1 | Linux default with no `set_start_method()` call (3.15 series, ≥3.15.1) | `forkserver` | forkserver bullet, "The default on those…"; "Changed in version 3.14: This became the default start method on POSIX platforms." |
| 2 | Linux default before 3.14 | `fork` | "Changed in version 3.14: On POSIX platforms the default start method was changed from fork to forkserver… See gh-84559." |
| 3 | Condition making the default `spawn` | No writable temporary directory (`tempfile.gettempdir()` not writable, e.g. read-only FS) | forkserver bullet, "…spawn is the default in that case"; "Changed in version 3.15.1…" (gh-155717) |

## How to confirm on a given machine

```python
import multiprocessing as mp

# 1. Before first need: None (global method not yet resolved)
print(mp.get_start_method(allow_none=True))   # None

# 2. Resolve the default and read it back
print(mp.get_start_method())                  # 'forkserver' on Linux (writable tmpdir)

# 3. The first entry of get_all_start_methods() is the default
print(mp.get_all_start_methods())             # e.g. ['forkserver', 'fork', 'spawn'] on Linux
```

To exercise the ask-3 condition, force an unwritable temp location before importing/starting anything, since the choice is made on first need:

```bash
# read-only or non-existent temp dir; tempfile.gettempdir() will not be writable
mkdir -p /tmp/ro_tmp && chmod 0555 /tmp/ro_tmp
TMPDIR=/tmp/ro_tmp python -c "import multiprocessing as mp; print(mp.get_start_method())"
# 3.15.0  -> forkserver, and Process.start() raises OSError
# 3.15.1+ -> spawn
```

## Caveats and scope

- **"Linux" = the POSIX class the docs describe.** The documentation does not have a Linux-specific paragraph; it says "POSIX platforms which support passing file descriptors over Unix pipes such as Linux." On Linux this is unconditionally satisfied, so the answer holds. It does *not* automatically hold for every POSIX system (the availability clause is a real precondition), and it does not apply to Windows.
- **macOS is a different case, not a counterexample.** "Changed in version 3.8: On macOS, the spawn start method is now the default." That predates and is independent of the 3.14 fork→forkserver switch.
- **Which 3.15 revision is authoritative.** The 3.15 docs page as fetched already carries the 3.15.1 change note, so it describes 3.15.1 and later point releases of the branch. Note that the in-development translation page https://docs.python.org/uk/dev/library/multiprocessing.html labels the same change "Changed in version 3.16" — that page tracks a development branch ahead of 3.15. The answers above are pinned to the 3.15 branch documentation, per the request. If a specific 3.15.x point release must be pinned, 3.15.0 differs only on ask 3 (see the version pin above).
- **Historical default read from current docs, not from 3.13 docs.** Ask 2 is answered from the 3.15 page's own "Changed in version 3.14" note (gh-84559), which states the prior default by name; no separate 3.13-era page was needed.
- **No repository, build, or execution is involved.** The verification snippets above are provided for a reader to run; nothing here was executed, and the answer rests entirely on the quoted documentation text.

# Kubernetes version-skew evaluation: kubelets vs. kube-apiserver v1.27

## 1. Governing rule (ask #1)

The applicable rule is the kubelet-to-kube-apiserver skew rule from the Kubernetes **Version Skew Policy** (kubernetes.io/releases/version-skew-policy/), quoted verbatim:

> **kubelet must not be newer than kube-apiserver.**
> **kubelet may be up to three minor versions older than kube-apiserver** (kubelet < 1.25 may only be up to two minor versions older than kube-apiserver).

Expressed for an apiserver minor version `n`:

```
supported kubelet minor versions = [n - 3, n]   (inclusive), with the exception:
  kubelet minor < 1.25  ->  [n - 2, n]
```

Two notes on scope, resolved explicitly since the request left them open:

- **"Supported" means natively supported skew** — i.e., the version pair lies inside the policy's tested/supported window — not "reachable by an upgrade path." An upgrade path exists for every version (upgrade the node), so that reading would make the question vacuous.
- **Policy-wording ambiguity.** The n-2 -> n-3 expansion (KEP-3935) took effect starting with **v1.25 nodes against v1.28 control planes**; at the time v1.27 was the newest minor, the rule in force was `kubelet ∈ [n-2, n]`. Both readings are evaluated below and **converge on the same answer for all three candidates**, so the ambiguity does not change the result.

Other components (kube-proxy, kubectl, controllers) and cluster-manager restrictions (e.g. kubeadm managing kubelets only one minor back) are out of scope per the request.

## 2. Evaluation procedure

Inputs: `n = 27` (kube-apiserver minor version). Candidates: `1.28`, `1.25`, `1.24`.

Procedure per candidate, parse `MINOR`, compute `d = n - MINOR`:

1. If `d < 0` (kubelet newer) -> OUT.
2. If `MINOR < 25` and `d > 2` -> OUT.
3. Else if `d > 3` -> OUT.
4. Else -> IN.

## 3. Worked results

| kubelet | d = 27 - MINOR | Rule applied | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **v1.28** | d = -1 (kubelet is **newer**) | "kubelet must not be newer than kube-apiserver" | **OUT** |
| **v1.25** | d = 2 (older) | 2 ≤ 3 permitted; kubelet is not < 1.25 so the two-version exception does not tighten it | **IN** |
| **v1.24** | d = 3 (older) | kubelet < 1.25, so the exception caps the gap at **2**; 3 > 2 | **OUT** |

Cross-check under the **older n-2 policy** (the wording in force when v1.27 was current): allowed set = [1.25, 1.27] -> v1.25 IN, v1.28 OUT (newer), v1.24 OUT (d = 3 > 2). Identical outcome.

### Supported window for this pairing

```
kube-apiserver = 1.27
supported kubelets = 1.27, 1.26, 1.25
```

None of the three candidates falls outside this window ambiguously: v1.28 is one minor *above* the ceiling 1.27; v1.24 is one minor *below* the floor 1.25; v1.25 is exactly the floor.

## 4. Answer (ask #2)

Of the listed kubelets, **only v1.25** is inside the supported skew against kube-apiserver v1.27.

- **v1.28 — not supported:** newer than the kube-apiserver; the policy permits kubelets to lag, never lead.
- **v1.25 — supported:** two minor versions behind, within the three-minor allowance (and within the stricter two-minor allowance that applied to older-than-1.25 nodes).
- **v1.24 — not supported:** three minor versions behind, but v1.24 is a kubelet < 1.25, which the policy caps at two minor versions behind an apiserver; it is also outside the n-2 window that governed v1.27-era clusters.

## 5. Qualifications (not changing the verdicts)

- **HA caveat:** if kube-apiserver instances are skewed (e.g. 1.27 and 1.26 during a control-plane rollout), the window narrows to the intersection across all apiservers; with 1.27/1.26 it becomes 1.26..1.25 for older nodes and v1.25 stays in, while v1.28 and v1.24 stay out.
- **Patch versions** do not affect the skew check; only major.minor matters.
- **Release support lifetime** is a separate axis from skew: a kubelet can satisfy the skew rule while its minor version is past end of life. The request asks only about skew, so v1.25's verdict is a skew verdict.
- **kubeadm** only manages kubelets one minor version older than the kubeadm build; that is a tool restriction, not the project skew policy.

## Answer

### 1. Port range used when `nodePort` is unset and no port-range flag is set

The kube-apiserver default for `--service-node-port-range` is:

**30000-32767, inclusive at both ends.**

So a `type: NodePort` Service with no explicit `nodePort` gets its node port allocated from the default range `30000-32767`. With the static-subrange behavior active, the initial dynamic allocation is taken from the upper band, `30086-32767`, and only falls back to the lower band, `30000-30085`, after the upper band is exhausted.

### 2. Default split into static and dynamic bands

For the default range `30000-32767`:

| Band | Range | Size | Role |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Static band | `30000-30085` | 86 ports | Lower band, intended for explicit/static `nodePort` requests; low collision risk because dynamic allocation avoids it until the upper band is exhausted. |
| Dynamic band | `30086-32767` | 2682 ports | Upper band, the default source for automatically assigned node ports. |

So the split is:

- **Static band: `30000-30085`**
- **Dynamic band: `30086-32767`**

Dynamic allocation uses the upper band first. Once the upper band is exhausted, the allocator may use the lower/static band.

## Calculation

Using the documented formula:

```text
range size = 32767 - 30000 + 1 = 2768
band offset = min(max(16, floor(range size / 32)), 128)
            = min(max(16, floor(2768 / 32)), 128)
            = min(max(16, 86), 128)
            = 86

static band start = 30000
static band end   = 30000 + 86 - 1 = 30085

dynamic band start = 30086
dynamic band end   = 32767

dynamic band size = 32767 - 30086 + 1 = 2682
```

Check:

```text
86 static ports + 2682 dynamic ports = 2768 total ports
```

The bands are contiguous and non-overlapping: `static end + 1 = dynamic start`.

Note: the KEP example computes the range size as `32767 - 30000 = 2767` and shows the static band ending at `30086`. That is an exclusive-end diagram. The inclusive static end is `30085`, matching the current Service documentation.

## Important qualifications

- The static/dynamic subdivision is provided by the `ServiceNodePortStaticSubrange` feature. It was introduced as an alpha feature in Kubernetes 1.27 and is enabled by default in current releases where it has graduated. On clusters where the feature gate is disabled, or on releases before the feature, there is no static band: the entire `30000-32767` range is dynamically allocated. The default range itself remains `30000-32767`.
- The static band is not an exclusive reservation. An explicitly requested `nodePort` is validated against the whole configured range and must be free/unique; an explicit request in the dynamic band is allowed if that port is free. The static band is simply the lower-collision region that the dynamic allocator avoids until the upper band is exhausted.
- Existing node port allocations are not moved when the feature gate or range configuration changes; the policy affects new allocations.

## Verification

For a Service that has already been created, the allocated port is reported in:

```bash
kubectl get service <service-name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[*].nodePort}'
```

For the API server's configured range, inspect the kube-apiserver command line for `--service-node-port-range`; if the flag is absent, the default `30000-32767` applies.
