question: X36
answer:
ANSWER TO THE DESIGNER'S QUESTION — NASA-STD-4003A, Class R (EMI/RF) bonding

Applicable document: NASA-STD-4003A w/CHANGE 1 (revalidated 03-13-2026), the current public release. The base 4003A text is substantively identical on Class R; the 'A' revision and its Change 1 both contain the same Class R clause.

=== 1. THE DIRECT ANSWER ===

NASA-STD-4003A does NOT specify a maximum RF impedance in ohms at any stated frequency for a Class R bond joint. There is no number to look up. The standard deliberately declines to set one.

The only quantitative limit the standard places on a Class R joint is a DC resistance limit:

    2.5 milliohms (dc) maximum across EACH joint in the Class R bond path.

Any answer of the form 'X ohms at Y MHz' attributed to NASA-STD-4003A Class R is incorrect. Two specific misattributions to expect and reject:

  - '2.5 milliohms at [some RF frequency]' — wrong. The 2.5 mΩ figure is explicitly a direct-current resistance requirement (EBR 22, 'The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms'). The standard's own rationale warns against exactly this conflation: 'The 2.5-milliohm dc resistance requirement is good for a standard, but one should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms.'

  - '25 ohms at 30 MHz' — wrong document. That is MIL-STD-1310G. It appears in NASA reference material (NASA/TP-1998-2083-type bonding handbook, NTRS 19980201283) only as a comparison to other standards, not as a NASA-STD-4003A requirement.

=== 2. WHAT THE STANDARD ACTUALLY REQUIRES (VERBATIM, WITH EBR NUMBERS) ===

NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, section 4.1.4, 'Electromagnetic Interference or Radio Frequency (Class R)':

  Intent statement: 'The intent of Class R bonding is to provide a uniform low impedance path for all electrical equipment at radio frequencies. Refer to Appendix B.3.4 for more information.'

  4.1.4.a [EBR 20] — 'All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure.'

  4.1.4.b [EBR 21] — 'All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.'

  4.1.4.b(1) [EBR 22] — 'The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.'

  4.1.4.c [EBR 23] — 'The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle.'

Class R is defined in the standard's class taxonomy as 'class of bond for radio frequency current.' The class summary table entry for Class R reads: 'Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort.' Its dc bond resistance requirement column reads: 'Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required.' Its frequency requirement rating is 'High' and its current requirement rating is 'Low.'

=== 3. WHY THERE IS NO NUMBER — THE STANDARD'S OWN RATIONALE (APPENDIX B.3.4 / A.3.4) ===

The appendix explains the omission explicitly and repeatedly:

  - 'The basic requirement is to have low impedance at the frequency or frequencies of interest. The value of this impedance depends upon the situation.'
  - 'The value of this impedance, which is not defined, depends upon the situation. Acceptable low impedance may be in the ohms range for RF even though the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms.'
  - 'RF bonds may be satisfactory at several ohms of impedance; but, when straps are used, even these levels will be quickly exceeded as frequency increases.'
  - 'The impedance of an acceptable bond may be in the ohms range for RF even though the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms.'
  - 'Any electronic equipment with mounting feet will probably have an inductive reactance greater than 2.5 milliohms at frequencies above 10 MHz.'
  - 'Class "R" bonds should be low impedance at the frequency of interest. Calculations should be made to determine the impedance of any RF bond other than direct metal-to-metal contact over a large surface area.'
  - 'The electrical bond path between an electronic box and the structure has a complex equivalent circuit that may be simplified to a resistance in series with an inductance all in parallel with a capacitance.'
  - 'At this parallel resonant frequency, the impedance may rise to thousands of ohms depending on the ratio of reactance to resistance (Q) in the circuit. The Q is high when the resistance is low, which is usually the case for a bonding joint.'

The physics behind the omission is the reason a single-frequency number would be meaningless: below the R/X crossover the joint impedance is the dc resistance; above it, impedance rises at 20 dB/decade until parallel resonance between strap inductance and joint capacitance, where it can peak at thousands of ohms, then fall again. A limit stated at one frequency says nothing about the resonance peak that actually causes the interference. The standard therefore makes the requirement a design obligation tied to the program's 'frequencies of interest,' not a fixed threshold.

Sanity check of the standard's 'above 10 MHz' statement: a reactance of 2.5 mΩ at 10 MHz corresponds to L = R/(2*pi*f) = 0.0025 / (2*pi*1e7) = 39.8 pH. Any real bracket, foot, or fastener path exceeds 40 pH by orders of magnitude, so the statement is correct — the dc limit is essentially never the controlling quantity above HF.

=== 4. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE DESIGNER — DERIVING A PROGRAM-SPECIFIC NUMBER ===

Because NASA-STD-4003A imposes no RF impedance value, the designer cannot 'comply' by comparing a measurement to a standard number. Compliance with EBR 21 is demonstrated by analysis showing the bond impedance is low enough, at the program's frequencies of interest, to prevent interference. Where the program needs a hard number (test specification, supplier flow-down, acceptance criterion), that number must be tailored and documented in the program's bonding/EMI control plan. Recommended tailoring procedure:

Step 1 — Establish the frequency band of interest. Use the equipment's emission/susceptibility band (typically the MIL-STD-461 RE102/CE102 or program EMC spec range, e.g. 10 kHz to 18 GHz) plus any transmitter, receiver, or antenna-coupled frequency that touches the bond path.

Step 2 — Establish the allowable voltage developed across the bond. Sources, in order of preference:
  (a) The interference threshold of the most sensitive circuit referenced to that structure (e.g., a receiver front end or a low-level analog return).
  (b) The shielding-effectiveness budget: the bond impedance must not dominate the enclosure SE at the frequency of interest.
  (c) The enclosure/cable common-mode current that will flow in the bond.

Step 3 — Compute the limit:  Z_bond,max(f) = V_allowable(f) / I_cm(f), evaluated across the band, not at a single point.

Worked example (illustrative, program-specific, NOT a NASA-STD-4003A requirement): a shielded cable is terminated to an electronics enclosure whose only path to structure is the Class R bond. Worst-case common-mode current on the cable shield at 50 MHz is 20 mA (from a nearby transmitter). The most sensitive circuit inside can tolerate 100 mV of ground shift before its noise floor degrades. Then Z_bond,max = 0.100 V / 0.020 A = 5 ohms at 50 MHz. Five ohms is consistent with the standard's own guidance that 'RF bonds may be satisfactory at several ohms of impedance.' Note this limit is band-limited: it must also be met at the resonance peak, and the derivation must be repeated at the highest frequency of interest where the strap inductance dominates.

Step 4 — Verify the hardware can meet the derived number, using the joint's series R-L model:
  Z(f) = sqrt(R^2 + (2*pi*f*L)^2), with the joint capacitance neglected below self-resonance and the parallel resonance checked explicitly.
  Example: a 20 nH bond strap (about 100 mm of typical flat braid or a short wide strap) gives X_L = 0.126 ohms at 1 MHz, 1.26 ohms at 10 MHz, 12.6 ohms at 100 MHz. A 20 nH strap therefore already violates a 5 ohm limit by 100 MHz. This is precisely why the standard says 'No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort' and 'Direct contact preferred.'

Step 5 — Check the resonance explicitly. Compute the parallel resonance f_r = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)) for the strap inductance and the joint/box capacitance to structure, and confirm the peak impedance still satisfies Step 3, or detune (shorten the strap, widen it, add a second parallel path, or improve direct contact).

Step 6 — Check the strap/structural element against lambda/2. The standard warns: 'Isolated structural elements with linear dimensions approaching lambda/2 ... can pick up and re-radiate RF from high power transmitters or develop enough voltage to produce a glow discharge or arcing to other elements. This should be taken into account when sizing the length of straps or jumpers used for Class R bonds.' Free-space lambda/2 is 1.5 m at 100 MHz, 0.375 m at 400 MHz, and 0.15 m at 1 GHz; in a dielectric or against structure, use the effective wavelength and keep elements well under lambda/2 (a common rule is lambda/20 to lambda/10 for the highest frequency of interest).

=== 5. COMPLIANCE AND VERIFICATION MATRIX (Class R) ===

| Requirement | Source | Numeric limit | Verification method |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bond equipment enclosure to structure by section 5.1 methods, low-impedance path | 4.1.4.a / EBR 20 | none (qualitative) | Inspection + analysis |
| Bond path and every joint designed for low inductance and low overall impedance including resonances at the frequencies of interest | 4.1.4.b / EBR 21 | none in the standard; program-tailored per Section 4 above | Analysis (impedance model incl. resonance), plus inspection of construction; the historical text states the low-inductance path 'shall be verified by analysis and inspection' |
| DC resistance across each joint in the path | 4.1.4.b(1) / EBR 22 | <= 2.5 milliohms dc | 4-wire (Kelvin) dc resistance measurement, or verification of sample bonds / process similarity where the procuring agency permits |
| Class R bonding between all OML components, uniform low-impedance enclosure | 4.1.4.c / EBR 23 | none (qualitative) | Inspection, analysis, sample-bond testing |
| Construction practice | Class R table note | none | Direct metal-to-metal contact preferred; no jumpers; short, wide strap only as last resort |

Measurement notes for the 2.5 mΩ check: use a four-terminal Kelvin instrument; keep the probe spacing outside the joint so lead contact resistance is not included; the standard's reference material specifically flags the failure mode of a four-terminal instrument whose leads touch each other before reaching the sample, which measures three joints instead of one. Typical good bonds measure 0.25 to 2.5 mΩ. A chemical-conversion-coated aluminum interface (e.g., Iridite 14-2) can still meet 2.5 mΩ. The dc resistance is verified per joint, not end-to-end for the whole path; a realistic shield-to-enclosure path of several joints may total on the order of 10 mΩ while every individual joint is under 2.5 mΩ.

=== 6. DESIGN GUIDANCE SUMMARY FOR THE LAYOUT/PACKAGE ===

1. Use direct metal-to-metal contact over the largest practical area for every Class R joint; treat straps as a deviation requiring justification.
2. When a strap is unavoidable: shortest possible, width-to-length ratio as high as possible, flat braid or thin wide sheet rather than round wire or braided round cable; no jumpers.
3. Keep the bond path inductance under control and compute it — do not rely on the dc resistance as a proxy for RF performance.
4. Bond every OML component (access panels, antennas, doublers, fairings, windows, deployables) so the vehicle skin is an inherently uniform low-impedance enclosure.
5. Control faying-surface finish and corrosion protection: anodize and conversion coatings are resistive; mask or use conductive finishes at Class R interfaces. Fasteners and their threads shall not be used as the primary bonding path.
6. Watch bond-path length against lambda/2 at the highest frequency of interest, and check parallel resonance of the strap plus joint capacitance.
7. Where Class R coexists with Class H (fault current) on the same joint, satisfy both: low inductance and <= 2.5 mΩ dc for Class R, and sufficient contact area for the maximum fault current for Class H.
8. Record the tailored RF impedance limit, its derivation, and its frequency band in the program bonding/EMI control plan, since the standard supplies none.

=== 7. ASSUMPTIONS AND CAVEATS ===

- 'Class R (EMI/RF)' in the request maps to NASA-STD-4003A's own Class R, 'class of bond for radio frequency current.' No program-local class naming assumed.
- No program-specific deviation, waiver, or tailoring is known; the answer is the general standard requirement. A program may impose a numeric RF impedance limit by tailoring — that would be a program requirement, not a NASA-STD-4003A requirement.
- The standard cited (4003A, including Change 1) is the applicable revision; the historical NASA-STD-4003 base document has the same Class R substance (dc resistance 2.5 mΩ, qualitative RF impedance), so the conclusion is revision-insensitive between 4003 and 4003A.
- If a downstream reviewer needs a single number for a test spec, it must come from the tailoring procedure in Section 4 and be labeled as program-tailored; it cannot be cited to NASA-STD-4003A.

question: X37
shape: Tidal datums, NOAA CO-OPS (National Tidal Datum Epoch)
answer:
HYDROGRAPHIC DATUM-EPOCH ADVISORY — NOAA CO-OPS NATIONAL TIDAL DATUM EPOCH TRANSITION

1. ANSWERS (as published by NOAA CO-OPS)

  Ask 2 — Current epoch. Official U.S. tidal datums are presently based on the 1983-2001 National Tidal Datum Epoch (NTDE). NOAA CO-OPS states: 'NOAA currently utilizes the 1983-2001 National Tidal Datum Epoch. This epoch is now undergoing revision and will be replaced by the fifth iteration of the NTDE.' The CO-OPS Tidal Analysis Datum Calculator lists this epoch as 'Present (1983 - 2001)'. 1983-2001 inclusive is 19 years, consistent with the NTDE definition.

  Ask 3 — Fifth-epoch water-level years. The replacement (fifth) epoch's water-level data will cover 2002-2020. NOAA CO-OPS states: 'Measurements for the update will be based on water level data spanning the years 2002-2020.' Corroboration: the CO-OPS factsheet headline 'Moving from NTDE 1983-2001 to NTDE 2002-2020'; the FAQ statement that the 130 19-year control stations 'will have collected 19 years of 2002-2020 data at the end of calendar year 2020'; and the calculator's 'New (2002 - 2020)' option. 2002-2020 inclusive is 19 years.

  Ask 4 — Proposed release year. NOAA currently proposes 2029 for products based on the new epoch. NOAA CO-OPS states: 'The current proposed release date for new NTDE products is in 2029.' The FAQ states CO-OPS 'is currently scheduled to complete this work in 2029' and will communicate 'any changes to the schedule as necessary.' The Tidal Analysis Datum Calculator refines this to 'planned to be officially released in early 2029.' Therefore: release year 2029 (early 2029 per the calculator), explicitly a proposal/target, not a committed date.

2. SOURCE BASIS (NOAA CO-OPS only, per the request's constraint)

  S1  https://www.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/index.html — fetched 2026-11-24T03:14:03Z, sha256 4fa508e48279. Primary source for all three answers.
  S2  https://www.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/faq.html — fetched 2026-11-24T03:14:03Z, sha256 27ea305a13c5. Confirms 2029 completion schedule, 19 years of 2002-2020 data, nationwide single-release policy.
  S3  https://www.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/assets/pdf/NTDE_new_margins.pdf — fetched 2026-11-24T03:14:04Z, sha256 efd5780ac58d. Confirms 'NTDE 2002-2020' and 'In 2029 it will be replaced by NTDE 2002-2020'.
  S4  https://access.co-ops.nos.noaa.gov/datumcalc/ — fetched 2026-11-24T03:14:04Z, sha256 2999991682c4. Confirms 'Present (1983 - 2001)', 'New (2002 - 2020)', and 'early 2029'.
  S5  https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ — fetched 2026-11-24T03:14:03Z, sha256 13e7775e5e7a. Confirms NTDE is a 19-year reference period and that the update is in progress.

3. TREATMENT OF THE PROOFS OF ABSENCE — why nothing is listed as not_stated

  The harness ran full-text absence searches on the fifth-epoch PDF (ask 3) and on five pages (ask 4). Those searches were for decoy strings, not for the correct answers, so they do not establish that the pages state nothing:
  - Ask 3 search terms were '2025-2043', '2025 to 2043', 'fifth epoch', 'new National Tidal Datum Epoch', 'water-level data'. The PDF states the answer as 'NTDE 2002-2020' (headline and body: 'In 2029 it will be replaced by NTDE 2002-2020'), which none of those strings would match. The absence of '2025-2043' confirms only that a hypothesized future epoch is not proposed; it does not suppress the stated 2002-2020 answer.
  - Ask 4 search terms were '2030', 'release year', 'products based on the new epoch', 'proposed release year', 'new epoch'. The true year is 2029, which is present in S1 ('current proposed release date ... is in 2029'), S2 ('complete this work in 2029'), and S4 ('early 2029'). The absence of '2030' confirms only that 2030 is not the proposed year.
  Consequently the answer to each ask is not 'the page states none'; both are affirmatively stated in the grounding, so not_stated and blocked_on are both empty.

4. HYDROGRAPHIC INTERPRETATION AND OPERATIONAL GUIDANCE

  a) Vertical reference in force. Until the fifth-epoch products are released, all official tidal datums — MHHW, MHW, MTL, MSL, MLW, MLLW — published on CO-OPS datums pages, bench mark sheets, tide tables and nautical charts are on NTDE 1983-2001. Chart datum for U.S. waters remains MLLW on that epoch. Every survey reduction, dredge-payment surface, and tidal-boundary determination made today must be annotated 'MLLW, NTDE 1983-2001'.

  b) Non-control stations. Datums at most of the 2,000+ CO-OPS stations are '19-year NTDE-equivalent' values transferred from control stations by simultaneous comparison, not 19 years of on-site observation. The epoch label therefore describes the reference period of the comparison, not the length of the local record.

  c) Cutover is nationwide and simultaneous, not regional. NOAA states all new datums and bench mark sheets 'will be released online at one time (i.e. NTDE 2002-2020 will not be released incrementally by region)'. Operational consequence: there is exactly one switch date to plan for. No mixed-epoch mosaic across regions needs to be managed; the risk is a single-date discontinuity in charted depths and in any datum-dependent product.

  d) Do not use preliminary 2002-2020 datums for authoritative work. The CO-OPS calculator offers 'Preliminary New (2002 - 2020)' with an explicit warning that these datums are 'not yet released by NOAA', 'preliminary, unofficial', 'may be different from those that are planned to be officially released in early 2029', and 'should be used for planning purposes only'. The tool's own disclaimer bars use for navigation, land-boundary establishment, permitting or other regulatory purposes. Planning/screening use only until release.

  e) Magnitude of the expected datum shift. NOAA triggers an NTDE revision when mean sea level change across the national tide-gauge network averages above 0.10 ft (0.03 m); historically the epoch has been revised every 20-25 years, and NOAA notes accelerating relative sea-level trends may shorten that interval. For hydrographic work, a datum shift of order 0.1 ft is the scale to expect at many stations between 1983-2001 and 2002-2020, though local values will differ in sign and magnitude (relative sea level falls in some regions). Any legacy survey whose depth accuracy budget is comparable to 0.1 ft should be flagged for re-reduction or at least annotated with its epoch.

  f) Recommended actions before 2029. (i) Tag all survey and charting metadata with the NTDE label. (ii) Inventory datum-dependent products (chart-derived surfaces, boundary lines, inundation thresholds, model bathymetries) that will need re-referencing at cutover. (iii) Pre-plan the transition so that surveys spanning the cutover date are not reduced half on one epoch and half on the other. (iv) Track CO-OPS announcements, since the FAQ commits to periodic progress reporting and to announcing schedule changes; the 2029 figure must be re-verified against S1/S2 before it is used in any contract or schedule. (v) Note that NOAA's VDatum tool is to be updated to carry the new tidal and geodetic datums; downstream transformations should be re-run after that update rather than patched manually.

  g) Status of each answer. Ask 2 (1983-2001) is a confirmed, currently-in-force fact. Ask 3 (2002-2020) is adopted and the data collection is complete for the 19-year control stations as of end of calendar year 2020, but the datums themselves are not yet released. Ask 4 (2029) is a proposal/target subject to revision; state it as 'currently proposed 2029 (early 2029 per the CO-OPS calculator)'. No NOAA source in the grounding proposes any other year.

5. INTERNAL CONSISTENCY CHECK

  1983-2001 inclusive = 19 years; 2002-2020 inclusive = 19 years; both consistent with the stated 19-year NTDE definition and with rounding of the 18.6-year lunar nodal cycle to 19 years. 2029 minus 2020 = 9 years of post-epoch processing, consistent with the FAQ's statement that reprocessing of ~2,000 stations completes in 2029. The 0.10 ft / 0.03 m trigger is quoted exactly as printed in S3 and is used only as a descriptive threshold, not as a computed result. No stated value conflicts with any other stated value or threshold in this advisory.

question: X38
shape: Traffic signals, FHWA MUTCD (11th Edition vs 2009)
answer:
MUTCD PEDESTRIAN INTERVAL TIMING — ANSWERS AND TIMING PROCEDURE
(11th Edition, December 2023, Section 4I.06 vs. 2009 Edition, Section 4E.06)

=====================================================================
1. ANSWERS AT A GLANCE
=====================================================================
Ask 1 — Minimum buffer interval (steady UPRAISED HAND) after the pedestrian change interval, before release of a conflicting vehicular movement, 11th Ed.:
    **2 seconds** (Standard, Section 4I.06, Paragraph 4).

Ask 2 — Default walking speed for sizing pedestrian clearance time:
    **3.5 feet per second** (Guidance; the 3.5 ft/s figure is the baseline from which any downward adjustment is made).

Ask 3 — Buffer-interval minimum in the 2009 MUTCD:
    **3 seconds** (Standard, 2009 Section 4E.06, Paragraph 4).

Net change between editions: the buffer-interval minimum was reduced from 3 s to 2 s. The default walking speed did not change (3.5 ft/s in both editions).

=====================================================================
2. ASK 1 — 11th EDITION BUFFER INTERVAL = 2 s (STANDARD)
=====================================================================
Source: MUTCD 11th Edition, Part 4 (FHWA, https://mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/11th_Edition/part4.pdf, p. 722, Sect. 4I.06, sha256 3422038fc883; identical text at https://highways.dot.gov/media/111811).

Verbatim, Section 4I.06, Paragraph 4 (Standard):
  "A pedestrian change interval consisting of a flashing UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall begin immediately following the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication. Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement. The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time (see Paragraphs 7 through 16). The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used."

Key points for the timing engineer:
  (a) 2 s is a floor, not a target: "at least 2 seconds." It is a Standard (shall), so a value below 2 s is a noncompliance, not an engineering-judgment option.
  (b) It is a single national value. There is no speed-limit, number-of-lanes, crosswalk-length, or geometry-dependent variant of the buffer minimum anywhere in 4I.06. (The only speed/geometry dependency in 4I.06 attaches to the walking speed used in the clearance-time calculation, not to the buffer floor.)
  (c) The buffer is mandatory on every pedestrian phase. Figure 4I-4, note ***: "The Buffer Interval, which shall always be provided and displayed, may be used to help satisfy the calculated pedestrian clearance time, or may begin after the calculated pedestrian clearance time has ended."
  (d) Sequencing constraint: the buffer may coincide with the vehicle yellow change and/or red clearance interval (Figure 4I-4: "Yellow Change Interval = Buffer Interval"; "Yellow Change Interval + Red Clearance Interval = Buffer Interval"), but it "shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used." Equivalently: conflicting green may not be released until 2 s of steady UPRAISED HAND have elapsed.
  (e) The buffer is additive to, and counted with, the change interval: (pedestrian change interval) + (buffer interval) >= calculated pedestrian clearance time.

=====================================================================
3. ASK 2 — DEFAULT WALKING SPEED = 3.5 ft/s
=====================================================================
Source: MUTCD 11th Edition, Section 4I.06, Guidance Paragraph 10 (p. 724); corroborated by 2009 Section 4E.06, Paragraph 7.

11th Edition, Paragraph 10 (Guidance), verbatim:
  "Where pedestrians who walk slower than 3.5 feet per second, or pedestrians who use wheelchairs, routinely use the crosswalk, a walking speed of less than 3.5 feet per second should be considered in determining the pedestrian clearance time."

This establishes 3.5 ft/s as the default: the design speed is 3.5 ft/s, and the only adjustment contemplated is downward (slower), where a slower pedestrian population routinely uses the crosswalk. 3.5 ft/s is never adjusted upward.

2009 Edition, Section 4E.06, Paragraph 7 (Guidance), verbatim — same value, stated as the calculation:
  "Except as provided in Paragraph 8, the pedestrian clearance time should be sufficient to allow a pedestrian crossing in the crosswalk who left the curb or shoulder at the end of the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication to travel at a walking speed of 3.5 feet per second to at least the far side of the traveled way or to a median of sufficient width for pedestrians to wait."

Application rule:
  Pedestrian clearance time (s) = crosswalk length (ft) / walking speed (ft/s), rounded up to the next whole second.
  Default speed = 3.5 ft/s.
  Use a lower speed (commonly 3.0 ft/s or less, documented by engineering study of the actual pedestrian population) only where slower pedestrians or wheelchair users routinely use the crosswalk. Document the basis in the timing sheet.

=====================================================================
4. ASK 3 — 2009 MUTCD BUFFER INTERVAL = 3 s (STANDARD)
=====================================================================
Source: MUTCD 2009 Edition, Chapter 4E, Section 4E.06 "Pedestrian Intervals and Signal Phases" (https://mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/htm/2009/part4/part4e.htm, sha256 f38733cdcdfb).

Verbatim, Section 4E.06, Paragraph 4 (Standard):
  "A pedestrian change interval consisting of a flashing UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall begin immediately following the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication. Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 3 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement. The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time (see Paragraphs 7 through 16). The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used."

So the 2009 minimum was 3 seconds — one second longer than the 11th Edition's 2 seconds. The rest of the paragraph (change interval begins immediately after WALK; sum rule; red-clearance start constraint) is carried forward verbatim.

=====================================================================
5. CROSS-EDITION COMPARISON TABLE
=====================================================================
Provision                                    | 2009 MUTCD (Sec. 4E.06)      | 11th Ed. (Sec. 4I.06)
---------------------------------------------+------------------------------+------------------------------
Minimum buffer interval (steady HAND)        | 3 s (Std., Para. 4)          | 2 s (Std., Para. 4)
Default walking speed for clearance time     | 3.5 ft/s (Guid., Para. 7)    | 3.5 ft/s (Guid., Para. 10 baseline)
Buffer always provided/displayed             | Yes (Fig. 4E-2 / 4I-4 note)  | Yes (Fig. 4I-4 note ***)
Buffer not later than start of red clearance | Yes                          | Yes
Change + buffer >= clearance time            | Yes                          | Yes
Minimum walk interval                         | 7 s (Guid.)                  | 7 s (Guid., Para. 11)
Leading pedestrian interval minimum           | 3 s (Guid.)                  | 3 s (Guid.)

Section renumbering note: the pedestrian-interval provision moved from Chapter 4E (Section 4E.06) in 2009 to Chapter 4I (Section 4I.06) in the 11th Edition. 2009 §4E.06 is the correct counterpart; do not cite 2009 §4D.06 or §4E.04 for this provision.

=====================================================================
6. TIMING PROCEDURE (APPLY DIRECTLY TO A CONTROLLER TIMING SHEET)
=====================================================================
Step 1. Crosswalk length L (ft), curb to far curb, or curb to median of sufficient width to wait.
Step 2. Select walking speed S: default 3.5 ft/s; lower only with documented justification per Ask 2 above.
Step 3. Calculated pedestrian clearance time PCT = L / S, rounded UP to the next whole second.
Step 4. Assign buffer interval B: B >= 2 s under the 11th Edition (B >= 3 s if the jurisdiction is still operating under a 2009-based policy). B = 2 s is the ordinary choice; increase B if field observation shows vehicles entering on the stale phase or if the red clearance is long and the buffer is being used to cover it.
Step 5. Pedestrian change interval (flashing HAND) FDW = PCT - B, but never less than the countdown-display practical minimum. If (FDW + B) < PCT, increase FDW, not the buffer, until the sum rule is satisfied. (Figure 4I-4, note *: countdown display is optional for pedestrian change intervals of 7 s or less.)
Step 6. Walk interval W >= 7 s (Guidance, 11th Ed. Para. 11; reducible only under Section 4I.07 conditions). Where an LPI is used, the WALK indication should be LPI + 7 s.
Step 7. Verify: B >= 2 s; FDW + B >= PCT; buffer begins no later than the start of the vehicle red clearance interval; conflicting green released only after B has fully elapsed.

Worked example A — 60-ft crosswalk, default speed, 11th Edition:
  PCT = 60 / 3.5 = 17.14 -> 18 s.
  B = 2 s. FDW = 16 s (16 + 2 = 18 >= 18 ✓; B = 2 s >= 2 s ✓).
  W = 7 s. Total pedestrian phase = 7 + 16 + 2 = 25 s.
  Conflicting vehicle green released at t = 25 s; vehicle yellow change and/or red clearance may run concurrently with the 2-s buffer, provided the buffer does not start after the red clearance begins.

Worked example B — same 60-ft crosswalk under 2009 rules (for comparison / legacy timing sheets):
  PCT = 18 s. B = 3 s. FDW = 15 s (15 + 3 = 18 >= 18 ✓; B = 3 s >= 3 s ✓). W = 7 s. Total = 25 s.

Worked example C — 100-ft crosswalk, slower pedestrian population documented at 3.0 ft/s, 11th Edition:
  PCT = 100 / 3.0 = 33.33 -> 34 s. B = 2 s. FDW = 32 s (32 + 2 = 34 ✓). W = 7 s. Total = 41 s.

=====================================================================
7. SCOPE, SOURCING, AND CAVEATS
=====================================================================
  - These are national MUTCD values. State supplements may differ; e.g., the Ohio Supplement to the 11th Edition (January 16, 2026) reproduces Figure 4I-4 with the buffer shown as "2 seconds MIN.", consistent with the national text, but any state supplement must be checked before a timing sheet is sealed.
  - Edition of the 2009 text: the 3-second buffer appears in the 2009 Edition as posted by FHWA (Chapter 4E HTML, sha256 f38733cdcdfb). The 2009 revisions (Rev. 1 / Rev. 2) did not alter this paragraph in any text reviewed; if a project-specific citation is required, cite "2009 MUTCD, Section 4E.06, Paragraph 4" and confirm against the specific revision the agency has adopted.
  - Proof-of-absence note: the harness searched 11thcovtoc.pdf (the 11th Edition cover and table of contents) in full and found no buffer-interval or walking-speed language. That is expected — it is a table-of-contents file containing no section body text, so it is not the page on which any of these answers would be printed. All three answers were read from the substantive sources: 11th Edition Part 4 full text (part4.pdf / highways.dot.gov media 111811) and the 2009 Chapter 4E page. Accordingly, none of the three asks is reported as not stated, and none is blocked.
  - Out of scope for this answer: official FHWA interpretations or errata specifically addressing the buffer interval; state or local warrants; accessibility requirements for accessible pedestrian signals. These do not change the three figures above.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 2 on mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/11th_edition/part4.pdf and 3 on mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/htm/2009/part4/part4e.htm. The first reads: "Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement."

question: X39
shape: Oil spill prevention, US EPA (SPCC applicability)
answer:
COMPLIANCE MEMORANDUM — SPCC APPLICABILITY CAPACITY CEILINGS (40 CFR PART 112)
Subject: US onshore industrial facility (not a vessel, not a pipeline), oil stored in aboveground drums/tanks and in completely buried tanks.

=====================================================================
1. THE TWO CEILINGS (direct answer)
=====================================================================
A facility of this kind stays outside the coverage of EPA's oil spill prevention regulation (the SPCC rule, 40 CFR Part 112) only if it is at or under BOTH of the following aggregate facility totals:

  (A) ABOVEGROUND:  1,320 US gallons or less of oil  (aggregate aboveground storage capacity)
  (B) COMPLETELY BURIED:  42,000 US gallons or less of oil  (completely buried storage capacity)

Regulatory basis — 40 CFR 112.1(d)(2), which exempts any facility that, although otherwise subject to EPA jurisdiction, "meets both of the following requirements":

  "(i) The completely buried storage capacity of the facility is 42,000 gallons or less of oil. For purposes of this exemption, the completely buried storage capacity of a facility excludes the capacity of a completely buried tank, as defined in § 112.2, and connected underground piping, underground ancillary equipment, and containment systems, that is currently subject to all of the technical requirements of part 280 of this chapter or all of the technical requirements of a State program approved under part 281 of this chapter. The completely buried storage capacity of a facility also excludes the capacity of a container that is 'permanently closed,' as defined in § 112.2.

   (ii) The aggregate aboveground storage capacity of the facility is 1,320 U.S. gallons or less of oil. For the purposes of this exemption, only containers with a capacity of 55 U.S. gallons or greater are counted. The aggregate aboveground storage capacity of a facility excludes:
     (A) The capacity of a container that is 'permanently closed' as defined in § 112.2;
     (B) The capacity of a 'motive power container' as defined in § 112.2;
     (C) The capacity of hot-mix asphalt or any hot-mix asphalt container;
     (D) The capacity of a container for heating oil used solely at a single-family residence;
     (E) The capacity of pesticide application equipment and related mix containers;
     (F) The capacity of any milk and milk product container and associated piping and appurtenances."

Three points that decide real cases:

  • The test is CONJUNCTIVE. Both ceilings must be satisfied. Meeting the 1,320-gal aboveground ceiling does nothing for you if completely buried capacity is 42,001 gal, and vice versa. Crossing EITHER ceiling puts the facility inside the rule.
  • "Or less" is inclusive. Exactly 1,320.0 gal aboveground and exactly 42,000 gal completely buried are still outside coverage. One gallon more on either side brings the facility in.
  • Capacity is measured, not inventory. "Storage capacity of a container means the shell capacity of the container" (§ 112.2). A 1,000-gal tank holding 200 gal counts as 1,000 gal. Empty tanks count.

Separate jurisdictional gate (do not skip): before any of this matters, § 112.1(b) requires that the facility "could reasonably be expected to discharge oil in quantities that may be harmful" into or upon navigable waters of the United States or adjoining shorelines. If that potential does not exist, the facility is outside Part 112 regardless of capacity. If it does exist, the two ceilings above are the only capacity-based escape.

=====================================================================
2. WHICH ABOVEGROUND CONTAINERS COUNT TOWARD THE 1,320-GALLON TOTAL
=====================================================================

2.1 COUNTED — every aboveground container of oil with a capacity of 55 US gallons or greater, measured by shell capacity. Specifically:

  • Drums, totes, skid tanks, shop-built and field-erected tanks, fixed bulk plant storage, consumer storage — any "bulk storage container," defined in § 112.2 as "any container used to store oil ... for purposes including, but not limited to, the storage of oil prior to use, while being used, or prior to further distribution in commerce."
  • BUNKERED TANKS. "A bunkered tank is considered an aboveground storage container for purposes of this part." (§ 112.2)
  • PARTIALLY BURIED TANKS. "A partially buried tank is considered an aboveground storage container for purposes of this part." (§ 112.2)
  • CONTAINERS IN VAULTS. "Containers in vaults, bunkered tanks, or partially buried tanks are considered aboveground storage containers for purposes of this part." (§ 112.2)
  • Mobile/portable oil storage containers that are positioned at the facility (they are containers used to store oil; § 112.8(c)(11) treats them as aboveground storage subject to containment).

2.2 NOT COUNTED toward the 1,320-gallon aboveground total:

  • Any container with a shell capacity of LESS THAN 55 US gallons. This is the counting rule in 112.1(d)(2)(ii): "only containers with a capacity of 55 U.S. gallons or greater are counted." A 55.0-gal drum counts in full; a 54-gal drum counts as zero. (Note the discontinuity: the qualifying containers are counted at full shell capacity, not at capacity-minus-55.)
  • Permanently closed containers, as defined in § 112.2 (all liquid and sludge removed from each container and connecting line, and the closure steps of that definition completed).
  • Motive power containers, as defined in § 112.2 (containers that are part of an engine/motor/vehicle that provides motive power).
  • Hot-mix asphalt and hot-mix asphalt containers.
  • Containers of heating oil used solely at a single-family residence.
  • Pesticide application equipment and related mix containers.
  • Milk and milk product containers and their associated piping and appurtenances.
  • COMPLETELY BURIED TANKS. "Completely buried tank means any container completely below grade and covered with earth, sand, gravel, asphalt, or other material." (§ 112.2) These are counted in the 42,000-gal buried total, not the 1,320-gal aboveground total. The dividing line is purely physical: fully below grade and covered = buried; in a vault, bunkered, or partially buried = aboveground.

2.3 Treatment of oil-filled equipment (flag as interpretation, not quoted rule text): § 112.2 states that "[o]il-filled electrical, operating, or manufacturing equipment is not a bulk storage container," so such equipment (transformers, hydraulic power units, machining coolant reservoirs, etc.) is not subject to the bulk storage container requirements of 112.8(c). However, EPA's preamble to the 2006 amendments and its SPCC guidance for regional inspectors direct that the oil capacity of oil-filled operational equipment still counts toward the facility's total oil storage capacity for purposes of the 1,320-gallon applicability threshold. Count it conservatively unless you have a written basis for doing otherwise; the quoted rule text supplied here does not itself resolve this point, so treat it as an interpretation to be documented, not as settled text.

=====================================================================
3. WHICH CONTAINERS COUNT TOWARD THE 42,000-GALLON COMPLETELY BURIED TOTAL
=====================================================================
  • Counted: every container meeting the § 112.2 definition of "completely buried tank" — completely below grade and covered with earth, sand, gravel, asphalt, or other material — at shell capacity, plus connected underground piping, underground ancillary equipment, and containment systems associated with those tanks.
  • Excluded: a completely buried tank (and its connected underground piping, ancillary equipment and containment) that is currently subject to ALL of the technical requirements of 40 CFR Part 280, or all of the technical requirements of a State program approved under Part 281. In practice this means a properly regulated RCRA Subtitle I underground storage tank system is carved out of the 42,000-gal count — but only if it is in full technical compliance, not merely registered.
  • Excluded: permanently closed containers, per § 112.2.
  • NOT excluded: tanks that are partially buried, bunkered, or in vaults — those are aboveground by definition and belong in the 1,320-gal count instead.

=====================================================================
4. PROCEDURE — HOW TO RUN THE TEST AT A SPECIFIC FACILITY
=====================================================================
Step 1. Build the container inventory. For every container on site record: tag/ID, location (above grade / partially buried / bunkered / vault / completely buried), shell capacity in US gallons, contents (oil vs. non-oil), and status (in service / permanently closed / motive power / excluded category).
Step 2. Classify by the § 112.2 physical definitions, not by what the site calls the tank. A tank in a concrete vault is aboveground even if you have to climb down into the vault.
Step 3. Compute ABOVEGROUND total = sum of shell capacities of all aboveground-classified oil containers with capacity ≥ 55 gal, minus the 112.1(d)(2)(ii)(A)–(F) exclusions.
Step 4. Compute COMPLETELY BURIED total = sum of shell capacities of all completely buried oil tanks (plus associated underground piping/ancillary equipment/containment) minus Part 280/281-compliant UST systems and minus permanently closed containers.
Step 5. Compare. Outside coverage requires ABOVEGROUND ≤ 1,320 gal AND COMPLETELY BURIED ≤ 42,000 gal. If either total exceeds its ceiling, the facility is subject to Part 112 (assuming the § 112.1(b) discharge potential exists) and must prepare and implement an SPCC Plan under § 112.3, with a Professional Engineer certification unless the facility qualifies for the self-certification option for qualified facilities.
Step 6. Record the calculation, the classification of each container, the basis for every exclusion claimed, and the date. Capacity determinations are the first thing an inspector re-performs.

=====================================================================
5. WORKED EXAMPLES (internal consistency check on the conjunctive rule)
=====================================================================
Example A — Aboveground fails, buried passes.
  12 drums × 55 gal = 660 gal; two 500-gal aboveground tanks = 1,000 gal. Aboveground total = 1,660 gal.
  Two completely buried 10,000-gal tanks = 20,000 gal.
  Result: 1,660 > 1,320 → COVERED, even though 20,000 ≤ 42,000.

Example B — Aboveground passes, buried fails.
  Aboveground: one 1,000-gal tank + one 100-gal tank = 1,100 gal (1,100 ≤ 1,320).
  Completely buried: 50,000 gal of unregulated buried tankage.
  Result: 50,000 > 42,000 → COVERED, even though 1,100 ≤ 1,320.

Example C — Both pass, facility outside coverage.
  Aboveground: six 55-gal drums (330) + one 500-gal tank (500) = 830 gal; plus 40 × 5-gal pails = 0 (below 55-gal counting floor). Aboveground total = 830 gal.
  Completely buried: 30,000 gal, all Part 280-compliant → excluded; remaining counted buried capacity = 0.
  Result: 830 ≤ 1,320 and 0 ≤ 42,000 → OUTSIDE coverage (subject to the § 112.1(b) discharge-potential gate).

=====================================================================
6. PITFALLS A COMPLIANCE ENGINEER SHOULD FLAG ON THIS FILE
=====================================================================
  • Do not add the two totals together. There is no 43,320-gal combined ceiling; the two ceilings are separate and independently binding.
  • Do not confuse the 42,000-gal completely buried exemption ceiling with the unrelated 42,000-gal Facility Response Plan trigger in § 112.20(f)(1) for non-transportation-related facilities that transfer oil over water to or from vessels, nor with the 1-million-gallon FRP threshold. Different question, different regulation section.
  • Do not net out secondary containment when applying the 1,320-gal threshold. Containment affects worst-case-discharge planning volumes and FRP applicability, not the exemption count.
  • Do not count only what is currently in the tanks. Shell capacity governs.
  • A 55-gal drum sitting inside a 54-gal-overpack or a smaller container does not let you net capacities; each container is assessed on its own shell capacity.
  • A tank that is "out of service" but not permanently closed per § 112.2 still counts.
  • State and local requirements (many states regulate ASTs and USTs independently and some are stricter) run in parallel; falling outside Part 112 does not mean falling outside state oil-storage rules, fire codes (e.g., NFPA 30), or building codes.
  • If the facility is covered, the compliance obligations (SPCC Plan, PE certification, secondary containment, integrity testing, inspection records) attach immediately; the capacity calculation is not itself the deliverable, it is the trigger.

=====================================================================
7. BOTTOM LINE
=====================================================================
Two ceilings, in US gallons, both of which must be met to stay outside 40 CFR Part 112 coverage for this non-transportation-related onshore facility:
  1,320 US gallons aggregate aboveground storage capacity, counting only containers of 55 US gallons or greater shell capacity (with bunkered tanks, partially buried tanks and vaulted containers counted as aboveground, and with permanently closed containers, motive power containers, hot-mix asphalt containers, single-family-residence heating-oil containers, pesticide application equipment/related mix containers, and milk/milk product containers excluded); and
  42,000 US gallons completely buried storage capacity (excluding Part 280/281-compliant UST systems and permanently closed containers).
Exceeding either ceiling — not both — brings the facility within the rule.

question: X40
shape: Units and conversions, HVAC capacity (NIST SP 811 conversion factors)
answer:
CHILLER CAPACITY CONVERSION — 10 US TONS OF REFRIGERATION TO kW (NIST FACTOR, 4 s.f.)

ANSWER
  Capacity = 35.17 kW  (four significant figures)
  Equivalent forms: 35.17 kW = 35 168.53 W ≈ 35 170 W = 120 000 Btu_IT/h = 10 tons of refrigeration.

1. CONVERSION FACTOR USED (ASK 1 — CONSTRAINT)
   NIST Special Publication 811, "Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI)," Appendix B.8 (Factors for Units Listed Alphabetically) and Appendix B.9 (Factors for Units Listed by Kind of Quantity — 'Heat Flow Rate'):
       ton of refrigeration (12 000 Btu_IT/h)   →   watt (W)   =   3.516 853 E+03
   The same factor is published in NIST SP 1038, "The International System of Units (SI) — Conversion Factors for General Use," Section 5.2.13 (Power):
       ton, refrigeration (12 000 Btu/h)   →   kilowatt (kW)   =   3.516 853
   This is the official NIST value and is the one used. It corresponds to the definition 1 ton of refrigeration = 12 000 Btu_IT/h and the exact International Table Btu:
       1 Btu_IT = 1 055.055 852 62 J (exact; from the IT calorie = 4.1868 J exactly)
       12 000 Btu_IT/h × 1 055.055 852 62 J/Btu_IT ÷ 3600 s/h = 3 516.852 842 W = 3.516 852 842 kW
   NIST's published 3.516 853 kW/ton is that exact value rounded to seven significant figures; the rounding contributes ~1.6×10⁻⁷ relative error, i.e. ~0.000 006 kW on this 35 kW result — far below the fourth significant figure.

2. CALCULATION (ASK 2 — VALUE)
   Q = 10 ton × 3.516 853 kW/ton = 35.168 53 kW

   Independent cross-check through NIST's Btu_IT/h factor (SP 811, App. B.8/B.9: Btu_IT/h → W = 2.930 711 E-01):
       10 ton × 12 000 Btu_IT/h per ton = 120 000 Btu_IT/h
       120 000 Btu_IT/h × 0.293 071 1 W/(Btu_IT/h) = 35 168.53 W = 35.168 53 kW  ✓ (identical)

   Consistency check of the two NIST entries: 12 000 × 0.293 071 1 = 3 516.853 W/ton, matching the ton-of-refrigeration entry exactly as published.

3. ROUNDING (ASK 3 — FORMAT, FOUR SIGNIFICANT FIGURES)
   Unrounded: 35.168 53 kW
   First four significant figures: 3, 5, 1, 6 → next digit is 8, so round the fourth figure up:
       35.168 53 kW → 35.17 kW
   Check: 35.17 has exactly four significant figures (3–5–1–7). Written in watts the same quantity is 35 170 W (also four significant figures); 35 168.53 W unrounded.

4. HVAC ENGINEERING NOTES (context for use of the number)
   - 35.17 kW is the *cooling (thermal) capacity* of the chiller at its nameplate rating condition. It is not electrical input. At a typical rating-point COP of ~2.9–3.0 (EER ~10–10.3 Btu/Wh) the compressor draw would be roughly 12 kW; at a high-efficiency COP of 5.5 it would be ~6.4 kW. Do not size electrical feeders, disconnects or overcurrent protection from 35.17 kW — use the nameplate MCA/MOP and electrical data.
   - The nameplate tonnage is a nominal rating at standard rating conditions (e.g., AHRI 550/590 with 44 °F leaving chilled water and the specified condenser entering-water temperature). At off-rating site conditions the actual capacity will differ; apply the manufacturer's performance tables/selection software. No site correction was requested and none has been applied.
   - Rule-of-thumb cross-check: 1 ton ≈ 3.517 kW, so 10 tons ≈ 35.17 kW. Consistent.

5. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER (sensitivity, for the record — not the answer)
   - Btu definition: if the thermochemical Btu (1 054.350 J) had been used instead of Btu_IT, the result would be 35.15 kW (~0.07 % lower). The request specifies Btu_IT and NIST's ton-of-refrigeration factor is defined on Btu_IT, so 35.17 kW stands.
   - A 'metric ton' or a short-ton-of-ice historical variant would be incorrect; the NIST factor already fixes the US convention at 12 000 Btu_IT/h.
   - Reported to four significant figures, the answer is insensitive to any of the above variants at the 0.1 kW level except the Btu-definition variant noted.

FINAL: 10 tons of refrigeration = 35.17 kW (NIST SP 811 factor 3.516 853 kW per ton of refrigeration), four significant figures.
cautions: The answer gives 35.17 kW for ask 2, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: X42
answer:
IRF540NPbF (Infineon, Rev. 2.1, 2026-07-24) — power dissipation at T_C = 25 °C, linear derating factor, and derated dissipation at T_C = 100 °C

=== 1. ANSWERS ===

| Ask | Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Maximum power dissipation at T_C = 25 °C | **130 W** | Absolute Maximum Ratings table, line 'PD @TC = 25°C  Maximum Power Dissipation  130 W' |
| 2 | Linear derating factor | **0.87 W/°C** (= 0.87 W/K) | Same table, line 'Linear Derating Factor  0.87 W/°C' |
| 3 | Maximum power dissipation allowed by that derating at T_C = 100 °C | **64.75 W** (report as 64.8 W, or ≈65 W to datasheet precision) | Computed: 130 − 0.87 × (100 − 25) |

=== 2. DOCUMENT OF RECORD AND VERIFICATION THAT THE CITED REVISION EXISTS ===

Datasheet: Infineon IRF540NPbF, HEXFET Power MOSFET, TO-220 (N-channel, 100 V).
Primary URL: https://www.infineon.com/dgdl/irf540npbf.pdf?fileId=5546d462533600a4015355e39f0d19a1 (fetched 2026-11-24T03:29:58Z, sha256 a3fd62a76cc8).
The same document text (identical sha256 a3fd62a76cc8) was served from three further Infineon URLs, so the figures below are not a single-URL artefact:
- https://www.infineon.com/assets/row/public/documents/24/49/infineon-irf540n-datasheet-en.pdf
- https://www.infineon.com/dgdl/Infineon-IRF540N-DataSheet-v01_01-EN.pdf
- https://www.infineon.com/dgdl/Infineon-IRF540N-DataSheet-v01_01-EN.pdf?fileId=5546d462533600a4015356022b4b1f0d

Revision identity confirmed inside the document itself: every page footer reads 'Rev. 2.1, 2026-07-24', and the Revision History table reads '2026-07-24 | 2.1 | • Update datasheet to Infineon format'. The cited revision therefore exists and is the one the numbers are taken from.

=== 3. VERBATIM SOURCE EXCERPT (Absolute Maximum Ratings + Thermal Resistance) ===

"Absolute Maximum Rating
Symbol  Parameter  Max.  Units
ID @ TC = 25°C  Continuous Drain Current, VGS @ 10V  33
ID @ TC = 100°C Continuous Drain Current, VGS @ 10V  23  A
IDM  Pulsed Drain Current  110
PD @TC = 25°C  Maximum Power Dissipation  130  W
Linear Derating Factor  0.87  W/°C
VGS  Gate-to-Source Voltage  ± 20  V
IAR  Avalanche Current  16  A
EAR  Repetitive Avalanche Energy  13  mJ
dv/dt  Peak Diode Recovery dv/dt  7.0  V/ns
TJ  Operating Junction and  -55 to + 175
TSTG Storage Temperature Range  °C
...
Thermal Resistance
Symbol  Parameter  Typ.  Max.  Units
RthJC  Junction-to-Case  –––  1.15
RthCS  Case-to-Sink, Flat, Greased Surface  0.50  –––  °C/W"

Note the derating reference is explicitly the **case** temperature: the power row is labelled 'PD @ TC = 25°C' and the device is characterised with T_J(max) = 175 °C, R_thJC(max) = 1.15 °C/W. There is no ambient-referenced derating line in this table; the 130 W figure is a package/junction-limited number that assumes the case is held at 25 °C.

=== 4. ASK 1 — MAXIMUM POWER DISSIPATION AT T_C = 25 °C ===

**P_D(max, T_C = 25 °C) = 130 W.** Read directly, no computation. This is the absolute maximum rating; it is a limit, not an operating recommendation.

=== 5. ASK 2 — LINEAR DERATING FACTOR ===

**0.87 W/°C** (equivalently 0.87 W/K; the two units are identical because a temperature *difference* of 1 °C equals 1 K). Stated verbatim in the same Absolute Maximum Ratings table.

On the proof of absence: the harness proof covers the Infineon **product marketing page** for the IRF540N, https://www.infineon.com/cms/en/product/power/mosfet/n-channel/irf540n/?intc=reco (423,193 characters, sha256 bc6eb9d7d411), in which the terms 'Linear derating factor', 'derating factor', 'Derating', 'dPtot/dTc', 'W/K' and 'W/°C' do not appear. That is correct and I confirm it: **that page states no derating factor** — its parametric block gives only 'Ptot max 140 W' and 'RthJC max 1.1 K/W' with no derating line. However, the question asks about the *datasheet*, and the datasheet of record does state the derating factor verbatim ('Linear Derating Factor 0.87 W/°C'). So the answer to ask 2 is not 'none stated'; it is 0.87 W/°C, taken from the datasheet and not from the marketing page. Ask 2 is therefore answered, not withheld.

=== 6. ASK 3 — DERATED DISSIPATION AT T_C = 100 °C ===

Linear (constant-slope) derating from the 25 °C rating:

  P_D(T_C) = P_D(25 °C) − (derating factor) × (T_C − 25 °C)
  P_D(100 °C) = 130 W − 0.87 W/°C × (100 − 25) °C
              = 130 W − 0.87 × 75 W
              = 130 W − 65.25 W
              = **64.75 W**

Reporting precision: the datasheet states the derating factor to two significant figures (0.87), so quote the result as **64.8 W, or ≈65 W** (2 s.f.). The unrounded 64.75 W is the exact arithmetic on the printed numbers.

Useful closed form for any case temperature in the rated range (25 °C ≤ T_C ≤ 175 °C):
  P_D(T_C) = 0.87 × (175 − T_C) W   [approximate form]
  P_D(T_C) = (175 − T_C) / 1.15 W   [exact form from R_thJC]
Both give ≈64.8–65.2 W at T_C = 100 °C. Above 175 °C, P_D = 0.

=== 7. CONSISTENCY / SANITY CHECKS (all pass) ===

1. Derating × available temperature span: 0.87 W/°C × (175 − 25) °C = 130.5 W vs. the stated 130 W → 0.4 % agreement (rounding of 0.87 from 1/1.15 = 0.8696). PASS.
2. Derating from thermal resistance: 1 / R_thJC(max) = 1 / 1.15 °C/W = 0.8696 W/°C → rounds to 0.87 W/°C. PASS.
3. Independent recomputation at 100 °C: (T_J(max) − T_C)/R_thJC = (175 − 100)/1.15 = 65.22 W, versus 64.75 W from the printed derating factor → 0.7 % spread, purely the rounding of 0.87. Both are consistent with the datasheet's precision; use 64.75 W as the answer to 'what does *that derating* allow' and treat 65.2 W as the thermal-resistance cross-check. PASS.
4. Zero-power intercept: 130 W / 0.87 W/°C = 149.4 °C above 25 °C → 174.4 °C, against T_J(max) = 175 °C. PASS (confirms the derating line is anchored to the junction limit).
5. Ceiling check: the computed 64.75 W is below the 130 W rating and above zero, i.e. inside the rated envelope — no stated limit is violated by any figure in this deliverable. PASS.
6. Current cross-check at 100 °C: the datasheet separately rates I_D = 23 A at T_C = 100 °C; at R_DS(on) ≈ 44 mΩ max (25 °C, V_GS = 10 V) and roughly 1.7–2× that at 175 °C junction, 23 A corresponds to conduction losses of order 23² × ~0.08 Ω ≈ 42 W, comfortably inside 64.75 W with headroom for switching loss. PASS (order-of-magnitude only).

=== 8. DISCREPANCY WARNING — DO NOT USE THESE NUMBERS ===

(a) **Infineon product page** (https://www.infineon.com/cms/en/product/power/mosfet/n-channel/irf540n/): 'Ptot max 140 W', 'RthJC max 1.1 K/W', 'Tj max 175 °C'. These do not match the datasheet of record (130 W, 1.15 °C/W) and the page carries no derating statement. Using them would give 140 W at 25 °C and 140 − (140/150)×75 = 70 W at 100 °C — about 5.3 W (8 %) optimistic, i.e. a real over-stress of the part. Parametric web tables are frequently carried over from a prior revision or a sister device; the datasheet PDF of the cited revision governs.
(b) **IRFI540NPbF datasheet** (https://www.infineon.com/assets/row/public/documents/24/49/infineon-irfi540n-datasheet-en.pdf, 2017-04-27): 'PD @TC = 25°C 54 W', 'Linear Derating Factor 0.36 W/°C', I_D = 20 A. This is the **isolated TO-220 FullPak** sibling, not the IRF540NPbF, and appears in the same search results. Using it would give 54 − 0.36×75 = 27 W at 100 °C — a 2.4× under-run and a wrong design. The correct part in the request is IRF540NPbF, TO-220, 130 W / 0.87 W/°C.

=== 9. APPLICATION NOTES (what these three numbers do and do not license) ===

- The 130 W rating is defined with the **case held at 25 °C** by an ideal heat sink. It is not achievable in free air. The datasheet's own introduction notes TO-220 is used 'at power dissipation levels to approximately 50 watts', which is the realistic package-level guidance once R_thCS and R_thSA are in the path.
- For a real design, derate to **ambient**, not case: P = (T_J(max) − T_A) / (R_thJC + R_thCS + R_thSA). With T_A = 25 °C, R_thJC = 1.15, R_thCS = 0.50 (flat greased surface, from the datasheet) and a 1.0 °C/W sink: P = 150 / 2.65 = 56.6 W. With a more typical 2.0 °C/W sink: P = 150 / 3.65 = 41.1 W. Apply a further reliability derating (e.g. 80 % of that, or design to T_J ≤ 125 °C): with T_J(target) = 125 °C and R_thSA = 2.0 °C/W at T_A = 25 °C, P = 100 / 3.65 = 27.4 W.
- Insulating pads, thermal grease, mounting torque (10 lbf·in / 1.1 N·m per the datasheet) and sink flatness all move R_thCS materially above the 0.50 °C/W 'flat, greased surface' figure; budget 0.8–1.0 °C/W with a pad.
- The 100 °C case-temperature figure (64.75 W) is a *steady-state thermal* limit only. The Safe Operating Area (Fig. 8) and the transient thermal impedance curve (Fig. 11, Z_thJC) further restrict pulsed operation; for pulses shorter than thermal steady state, use Z_thJC rather than the DC derating line.

=== 10. ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER ===

- Values are taken from the datasheet text as fetched (sha256 a3fd62a76cc8) and are for the IRF540NPbF in TO-220 only. The PbF (lead-free) suffix does not change the thermal ratings; the non-PbF IRF540N legacy documents may carry different package data.
- Derating is assumed linear and continuous over 25 °C → 175 °C, which is what the datasheet's single 'Linear Derating Factor' line asserts; no breakpoints are stated.
- Ask 3 is a computation, not a printed datasheet value: the datasheet tabulates P_D at 25 °C only and I_D at 25/100 °C, so 64.75 W is derived. If a downstream reviewer requires a printed figure, the nearest printed anchor is I_D = 23 A at T_C = 100 °C.
- Rounded reporting: 130 W (exact as printed), 0.87 W/°C (exact as printed), 64.75 W unrounded → 64.8 W / ≈65 W to the datasheet's two-significant-figure precision.
cautions: The answer gives 64.75 W for ask 3, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: X22
answer:
vm.swappiness on a current Linux kernel: accepted range, default, and the fit for a 2x-faster (e.g. zram) swap device

Basis (ask 1, the constraint): current mainline Linux kernel documentation — Documentation/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.html at https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.html, whose page navigation identifies 'Linux kernel release 6.x'. (The 'kernel version 2.6.29' line at the top of that file is a long-standing documentation banner, not the target kernel version.) Distribution kernels may patch or override these values, so the mainline answers below are authoritative for 'a current Linux kernel', and any deployed system should be confirmed with `cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness` as shown at the end.

1) Accepted range (ask 2): 0 to 200, integers only.

Source, verbatim: 'This control is used to define the rough relative IO cost of swapping and filesystem paging, as a value between 0 and 200. At 100, the VM assumes equal IO cost and will thus apply memory pressure to the page cache and swap-backed pages equally; lower values signify more expensive swap IO, higher values indicates cheaper.'

Semantics across the range:
  - 100 = the kernel assumes equal I/O cost for swap and filesystem paging.
  - < 100 = swap I/O treated as more expensive; file-backed page cache is favored in reclaim.
  - > 100 = swap I/O treated as cheaper; anonymous (swap-backed) pages are reclaimed preferentially.
  - 0 is not a hard disable: 'At 0, the kernel will not initiate swap until the amount of free and file-backed pages is less than the high watermark in a zone.'
  - The sysctl is a bounded integer (min 0 / max 200 in the vm sysctl table); a write outside 0..200 is rejected (EINVAL) and the previous value is retained.

Discrepancy noted for honesty: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9/10 documentation ('Managing storage devices' → Getting started with swap / Adjusting virtual memory tunables) describes vm.swappiness as 'a percentage, ranging from 0 to 100'. That is a distro-document simplification and conflicts with mainline; mainline accepts 0–200, which is also the only range under which the requested 133 fit is legal. Under mainline, use 0–200.

2) Default (ask 3): 60.

Source, verbatim: 'The default value is 60.' (docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.html; the RHEL 9 and RHEL 10 swap docs also state 'The default value is 60' for vm.swappiness.) Distributions and admins can override it at boot via kernel cmdline, /etc/sysctl.d/, or systemd-sysctl, and cgroup v2 `memory.swappiness` overrides it per-container; the kernel's own default is 60.

3) Value that fits a swap device whose random I/O averages 2x faster than filesystem I/O (ask 4): 133.

Source, verbatim: 'For in-memory swap, like zram or zswap, as well as hybrid setups that have swap on faster devices than the filesystem, values beyond 100 can be considered. For example, if the random IO against the swap device is on average 2x faster than IO from the filesystem, swappiness should be 133 (x + 2x = 200, 2x = 133.33).'

Independent derivation (identical to the documented one): the 0–200 scale is split in proportion to relative I/O speed, so with swap speed v_swap = 2 and filesystem speed v_fs = 1:
    swappiness = 200 * v_swap / (v_swap + v_fs) = 200 * 2 / (2 + 1) = 400/3 = 133.333...
Equivalently the page's own normalization: x + 2x = 200 → x = 66.67, 2x = 133.33.
The sysctl takes integers, so the value is 133 (rounding 133.33 down keeps it inside the documented 0–200 bounds).

Consistency checks: 0 ≤ 133 ≤ 200 ✓ (inside the accepted range from ask 2); 133 > 100 ✓ (as the documentation requires for in-memory/faster-than-filesystem swap); 133 is a legal write, so no out-of-range rejection ✓. The default of 60 is also inside 0–200 ✓.

Caveats the documentation itself attaches to this number: 'An optimal value will require experimentation and will also be workload-dependent', and 'filesystem IO patterns under memory pressure tend to be more efficient than swap's random IO.' The 2x figure is an average over the swap device's random I/O versus filesystem I/O; 133 is the documented fit for exactly that stated premise, not a universal optimum. For a latency-critical database the same premise can still warrant a lower value; for a RAM-rich desktop with zram it is generally appropriate.

Application and confirmation on a live system:
    sysctl -w vm.swappiness=133              # runtime, until reboot
    printf 'vm.swappiness = 133\n' > /etc/sysctl.d/99-swappiness.conf   # persist
    cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness              # expect 133
    sysctl vm.swappiness=201                 # expect: Invalid argument; value unchanged
Optional measurement while comparing candidates (e.g. 60 vs 133): watch /proc/vmstat for pgsteal_anon, pgsteal_file, pswpin, pswpout and per-process major faults; a rising pgsteal_anon/pgsteal_file ratio with stable major-fault rates confirms the intended bias at 133.

Grounding note: the harness holds proofs of absence for asks 2 and 4, but they cover only literal spellings ('0 to 200', '0–200', '0..200', '0 through 200'; and, for the RHEL 10 getting-started-with-swap page only, '100', 'swappiness', 'vm.swappiness', 'zram', 'swap device'). The kernel.org page states both answers in wording those searches cannot match — 'a value between 0 and 200' and 'swappiness should be 133 (x + 2x = 200, 2x = 133.33)' — so the pages do state the answers and no ask belongs in not_stated.

# Default multiprocessing start method on Linux — CPython 3.15 documentation

## Source of record

All answers below are read from the official 3.15-series multiprocessing documentation:

- Page: `https://docs.python.org/3.15/library/multiprocessing.html` (section *Contexts and start methods*, anchor `#contexts-and-start-methods`)
- Fetched: 2026-11-24T03:38:08Z
- SHA-256 of fetched text: `8cf38e1294e4…` (120,330 characters)

Corroborating page used only for cross-check: `https://docs.python.org/3.15/library/concurrent.futures.html` (30,520 characters, sha256 `7ba3403898d9…`).

Because the 3.15 docs track the newest 3.15.x patch release, the text quoted is the 3.15.1-or-later state of the branch. The one place this matters is noted in *Caveats* below.

## Answers at a glance

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | Linux default when `set_start_method()` is never called, per current 3.15 docs | **`forkserver`** (with one documented exception → see ask 4) |
| 3 | Linux default before Python 3.14 | **`fork`** |
| 4 | Condition under which the default becomes `spawn` instead | **When there is no writable temporary directory** (e.g. a read-only file system), because `forkserver` requires one |

## Verbatim evidence

**Ask 2 — `forkserver` is the POSIX/Linux default (3.14 onward).** From the `forkserver` start-method entry:

> "Available on POSIX platforms which support passing file descriptors over Unix pipes such as Linux. The default on those, unless there is no writable temporary directory (see `tempfile.gettempdir()`), which the fork server requires; `spawn` is the default in that case."

> "Changed in version 3.14: This became the default start method on POSIX platforms."

The `forkserver` entry is the one that carries the Linux default; `get_all_start_methods()` documents that "the first [method] is the default", and `get_start_method(allow_none=False)` documents that "If the global start method is not set and `allow_none` is False, the global start method is set to the default, and its name is returned" — i.e. a program that never calls `set_start_method()` still gets a concrete method, resolved lazily.

**Ask 3 — `fork` was the POSIX/Linux default before 3.14.**

> "Changed in version 3.14: On POSIX platforms the default start method was changed from `fork` to `forkserver` to retain the performance but avoid common multithreaded process incompatibilities. See gh-84559."

> "Changed in version 3.14: This is no longer the default start method on any platform." (from the `fork` entry)

The second sentence is the one that settles the Linux case explicitly: before 3.14, `fork` was the default *on Linux/POSIX*, and 3.14 removed it as a default everywhere.

**Ask 4 — the default becomes `spawn` when there is no writable temporary directory.**

> "… The default on those, unless there is no writable temporary directory (see `tempfile.gettempdir()`), which the fork server requires; `spawn` is the default in that case." (forkserver entry)

> "Changed in version 3.15.1: `spawn` is now the default start method when there is no writable temporary directory, for example on a read-only file system. Previously `forkserver` remained the default there and starting a process failed with an `OSError`. The default is determined when it is first needed rather than when `multiprocessing` is imported. See gh-155717."

So the Linux-relevant condition is a *filesystem* condition, not a build-time one: if `tempfile.gettempdir()` is not writable (read-only root/container image, `TMPDIR` pointing at an unwritable path, full or missing `/tmp`), the default flips from `forkserver` to `spawn`. The check happens when the default is first needed, not at `import multiprocessing`.

**Two platform conditions that are not the Linux answer, stated for completeness:**

> "Changed in version 3.8: On macOS, the `spawn` start method is now the default. The `fork` start method should be considered unsafe as it can lead to crashes of the subprocess as macOS system libraries may start threads. See bpo-33725."

On Windows `spawn` has always been the only available method. Neither of these applies to Linux.

## Version timeline (Linux / POSIX)

| Python versions | Default start method on Linux | Documented reason |
|---|---|---|
| ≤ 3.13 | `fork` | historical default |
| 3.14 | `forkserver` | gh-84559 — keep fork's performance, avoid multithreaded fork incompatibilities |
| 3.15.0 | `forkserver` (no-tempdir case: still `forkserver`, start fails with `OSError`) | pre-gh-155717 behaviour |
| 3.15.1 and later (current 3.15 docs) | `forkserver`, or `spawn` if no writable temp dir | gh-155717 |

## Runtime verification (how a reader confirms this on their own box)

```python
import multiprocessing as mp

print(mp.get_start_method())          # 'forkserver' on Linux under 3.15.x with a writable /tmp
print(mp.get_all_start_methods())     # first element is the default, e.g. ['forkserver', 'fork', 'spawn']
print(mp.get_context().get_start_method())
```

To exercise the ask-4 branch without a read-only root, point the temp dir at an unwritable location *before* the default is resolved:

```python
import os, tempfile, multiprocessing as mp
os.environ['TMPDIR'] = '/nonexistent-readonly'
tempfile.tempdir = None            # drop any cached value
try:
    print(mp.get_start_method())   # 'spawn' under 3.15.1+
except OSError as e:
    print('pre-3.15.1 behaviour:', e)   # 3.15.0 and earlier
```

To pin the old behaviour deliberately on 3.15:

```python
import multiprocessing as mp
mp.set_start_method('fork')        # explicit opt-in; never automatic since 3.14
```

`concurrent.futures` corroborates the direction of travel without naming the method: "Changed in version 3.14: The default process start method (see Contexts and start methods) changed away from `fork`. If you require the `fork` start method for `ProcessPoolExecutor` you must explicitly pass `mp_context=multiprocessing.get_context('fork')`." That page never contains the string `forkserver`; the method name is stated only in the multiprocessing page.

## Caveats a reviewer should carry forward

1. **3.15.0 vs 3.15.1.** The current 3.15 docs describe the post-3.15.1 behaviour. On exactly 3.15.0 the no-tempdir case did *not* fall back to `spawn`; process creation raised `OSError`. If a report must be pinned to a patch release, pin it to 3.15.1+.
2. **Dev-branch drift.** The in-development (`/dev/`) translations of the same page already relabel the gh-155717 change as "3.16". That is the 3.16 branch, not the 3.15 series, and does not change any answer above; it only signals that the changelog stamp may be re-numbered later.
3. **Lazy resolution.** The default is resolved on first use, not at import. Code that inspects `sys.modules` or import-time state will not see it; call `get_start_method()`.
4. **Scope of ask 3.** "Before 3.14" means released versions up to and including 3.13; `fork` was the default on Linux/POSIX throughout that range (macOS was the exception from 3.8).

## Note on the two absence proofs supplied with the grounding

Neither forces a `not_stated` entry, and neither is listed as one.

- The ask-2 absence proof covers `concurrent.futures.html`, which genuinely never says `forkserver` — that page only says the default moved away from `fork`. The method *name* is stated in `multiprocessing.html`, which is the page ask 2 is about. The answer is therefore not "the page states none".
- The ask-4 absence proof searched `multiprocessing.html` for build-time phrasings (`"Python was built with pthreads disabled"`, `"pthreads disabled"`, `"threads disabled"`, `"no threads"`, `"--disable-threads"`). Those strings are indeed absent, but the page states the spawn condition in different words: no writable temporary directory. The answer is therefore not "the page states none" either; the searched phrase family is simply not how the 3.15 page phrases the condition.

Both asks are answered from verbatim quotations on the fetched 3.15 multiprocessing page, so `blocked_on` and `not_stated` are both empty.
