question: X36
answer:
CLASS R (EMI/RF) BONDING IN NASA-STD-4003A — WHAT THE STANDARD ACTUALLY REQUIRES

Document of record: NASA-STD-4003A w/CHANGE 1, 'Electrical Bonding for NASA Launch Vehicles, Spacecraft, Payloads, and Flight Equipment', document date 2013-02-05, Change 1 dated 2016-01-19, revalidated 2026-03-13. This is the current issued revision on the NASA Technical Standards System; there is no later revision. Everything below is quoted or paraphrased from that document.

=====================================================================
1. BOTTOM LINE — THE THREE ANSWERS
=====================================================================

ASK 1 — Maximum RF impedance in ohms: NONE IS STATED. NASA-STD-4003A states no maximum RF impedance value in ohms, at any frequency, for a Class R bond joint. There is no RF impedance limit, no test frequency, and no RF impedance measurement method anywhere in the Class R requirements. Do not quote a number and attribute it to this standard.

ASK 2 — The format: a numeric RF bond limit would have to be written as

    |Z_joint(f)| <= X ohms   at   f = Y Hz

together with the measurement method and the point of measurement across the joint. NASA-STD-4003A supplies no X, no Y, and no RF measurement method, so that statement cannot be instantiated from this standard. Any (X, Y) pair you see attributed to NASA-STD-4003A is either from a different document (a program bonding spec, MIL-STD-464, a contractor standard) or is a derived value someone has mislabelled.

ASK 3 — Verdict on what the standard actually requires: Class R is a performance-based, design-requirements class, not a numeric-limit class. It imposes (a) a low-impedance path from equipment enclosure to structure, (b) a design requirement that inductance and overall impedance including resonances be low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest — the frequencies of interest are defined by the program, not by the standard — and (c) exactly one numeric per-joint limit: dc resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms. The 2.5 milliohm figure is a DC resistance limit, not an RF impedance limit, and it is the only number the standard gives you for a Class R joint.

=====================================================================
2. THE CLASS R REQUIREMENT SET, VERBATIM
=====================================================================

4.1.4a  Electromagnetic Interference or Radio Frequency (Class R)  [EBR 20]
  'All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in
   section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure.'
  -> Qualitative. No number.

4.1.4b  Electromagnetic Interference or Radio Frequency (Class R)  [EBR 21]
  'All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such
   that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent
   interference at the frequencies of interest.'
  -> The core RF requirement. Note three things: it is a DESIGN requirement (satisfied by
     analysis and inspection, not by a pass/fail meter reading); it explicitly includes
     inductance and resonance, not just resistance; and 'the frequencies of interest' is
     deliberately undefined in the standard — it is a program input.

4.1.4b(1)  Electromagnetic Interference or Radio Frequency (Class R)  [EBR 22]
  'The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed
   2.5 milliohms.'
  -> The only numeric limit. Units are milliohms, quantity is DC resistance, and the object
     is each individual joint in the path (not the whole path).

4.1.4c  Electromagnetic Interference or Radio Frequency (Class R)  [EBR 23]
  'The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R
   electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a
   uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle.'
  -> OML-specific, qualitative. No number.

Table 1 (Summary of Electrical Bonding Classes), Class R column, purpose of bond:
  'Protects equipment from RF emissions. Applies to equipment that could generate,
   retransmit, or be susceptible to RF. Includes antenna mounts and cable shield
   connections. Covers wide frequency range.'

Table 1, Class R design guidance:
  'Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers.
   Short, wide strap may be used as last resort.'

Verification requirements applicable to Class R:
  'The resistance requirement of all classes of bonds shall be verified by testing sample bonds.'
  'Low inductance paths of Class R and Class L bonds shall be verified by analysis and inspection.'
  'The resistance of bonds may be measured on flight vehicles, but it is usually impractical to
   measure inductance or current carrying capability.'
  -> This is decisive for the designer's question: the standard's own verification scheme does
     not contemplate a flight RF impedance measurement. Resistance is measured; inductance and
     impedance are analysed and inspected.

Guidance/rationale material (the standard states in Section 4 that Appendix B carries the
reasons for requirements and data for modifications or waivers), includes:
  'A realistic value would be on the order of 10 milliohms from the shield to the electronics
   enclosure for a cadmium-plated aluminum assembly, with 2.5 milliohms maximum for any
   particular joint.'
  -> Read this correctly: 10 milliohms is a PATH total (shield to enclosure, i.e. several
     joints plus the shield termination), and it is guidance, not a requirement. The binding
     requirement is still 2.5 milliohms per joint. It is also still a DC figure. It does not
     create an RF impedance limit and it does not conflict with EBR 22.

Related: 4.1.4.1 is titled 'Electrical Connectors and Shield Termination' as of Change 1 (the
Change 1 summary shows the title changed from 'Electrical Connectors'). Shield terminations and
antenna mounts are explicitly named in Table 1 as Class R subjects, so they are in scope for the
design measures below even though the standard gives them no separate numeric limit.

=====================================================================
3. WHY THE STANDARD IS WRITTEN THIS WAY (and why you cannot extract a number)
=====================================================================

An RF bond limit is meaningless without a frequency and a geometry: the same joint is
milliohms at 10 kHz and tens of ohms at 100 MHz, because inductance dominates. A single
published number would either be trivially satisfied (useless) or impossible (over-constraining).
NASA therefore made EBR 21 a performance requirement tied to 'the frequencies of interest', and
put the only hard number on the DC resistance of the joint, which is cheap to measure on samples
and is a good proxy for contact quality and corrosion/degradation. The RF behaviour is pushed
into analysis and inspection, where the program's actual emission and susceptibility environment
can be used.

Consequence for the designer: you must CREATE the numeric RF criterion for your program and own
it. You cannot cite NASA-STD-4003A for it.

=====================================================================
4. PROCEDURE — DERIVING A DEFENSIBLE CLASS R RF CRITERION
=====================================================================

Step 1. Fix the frequencies of interest. Take f1..fn from the program EMI/EMC control plan:
every emitter fundamental and harmonic on the vehicle (transmitters, DC/DC switching
frequencies and their harmonics, processor clocks, pyro/ordnance lines), plus every receiver band
and every susceptibility test band the unit must survive. Write the list down; EBR 21 is
unverifiable without it. Bound the top of the range as f_max.

Step 2. Fix the interference threshold. Either the receiver sensitivity (for a victim path) or
the radiated-emission limit at the relevant distance (for a source path). Express as a voltage
V_th across the joint or as an equivalent current I_noise in the path.

Step 3. Compute the allowable joint impedance:
    Z_allow(f) = V_th / I_noise(f)
For a shielded-cable path use a transfer-impedance budget instead: the series combination of
the shield surface transfer impedance Z_T(f) times cable length, plus the bond-joint impedance,
must keep the voltage on the internal conductor pair below the victim's threshold.

Step 4. Convert Z_allow into a strap/joint geometry limit. For a short strap the joint behaves
as R_dc + j*2*pi*f*L, with a corner frequency f_c = R_dc/(2*pi*L) above which inductance rules.
The requirement on the design is therefore:
    L <= Z_allow(f_max) / (2*pi*f_max)
and the strap must also stay electrically short (length < lambda/20 at f_max) so the lumped
approximation is valid, and must be checked for series resonance with the structure (EBR 21
explicitly calls out resonances; two parallel bond paths of different length can also form a
parallel resonance that raises impedance at one band — prefer one well-defined path, or analyse
the pair).

Step 5. Design preference order, straight from Table 1: direct metal-to-metal contact (no
jumper, no strap) first; short wide strap only as a last resort. Surface finish, plating
compatibility and corrosion control govern the joint's long-term resistance more than geometry
does — a joint that measures 0.3 milliohm on the bench and corrodes to 3 milliohm in service
fails EBR 22, and nothing in the RF analysis will have predicted it.

Step 6. Verify per the standard's own scheme: dc resistance of sample bonds by test (four-wire
Kelvin, >=1 A test current, probes across the joint only, not through it); low inductance by
analysis and inspection. Keep the analysis in the compliance folder — that analysis IS the
EBR 21 evidence.

Step 7. If the program requires a single number on a drawing, write it as a DERIVED requirement,
not as a NASA requirement, e.g.:
    'DERIVED FROM NASA-STD-4003A EBR 21. Bond joint Z_joint <= [X] ohms for f = [f1] to [f_max],
     by analysis per [analysis doc], and dc resistance <= 2.5 milliohms per EBR 22 by test.'
That sentence is auditable and honest. 'Per NASA-STD-4003A, Z <= [X] ohms at [f]' is not.

=====================================================================
5. WORKED EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE — THESE NUMBERS ARE DERIVED, NOT FROM THE STANDARD)
=====================================================================

Geometry: aluminium strap, length l = 10 cm, width w = 2 cm, thickness t = 0.1 cm.
Inductance, rectangular bar approximation (l, w, t in cm, L in nH):
    L = 2*l*[ln(2*l/(w+t)) + 0.5 + 0.2235*(w+t)/l]
      = 20*[ln(9.524) + 0.5 + 0.0469]
      = 20*[2.2538 + 0.5 + 0.0469] = 20*2.8007 = 56 nH

Strap dc resistance (Al, 2.65e-8 ohm-m, A = 0.02 m x 0.001 m = 2e-5 m^2):
    R = 2.65e-8 * 0.1 / 2e-5 = 0.13 micro-ohm
-> the strap metal is irrelevant; the 2.5 milliohm budget is entirely consumed by the joint
   interfaces and finishes.

Impedance of the strap alone (R_dc negligible):
    corner where X_L = 2.5 mOhm: f = 2.5e-3/(2*pi*56e-9) = 7.1 kHz
    |Z| at 100 kHz = 2*pi*1e5*56e-9 = 35 mOhm
    |Z| at 1 MHz   = 352 mOhm
    |Z| at 10 MHz  = 3.5 ohm
    |Z| at 100 MHz = 35 ohm
So a joint that comfortably passes the 2.5 milliohm DC test is already 35 milliohms at 100 kHz
and 35 ohms at 100 MHz. This is exactly why EBR 22 alone cannot be used as an RF criterion, and
why EBR 21 is a separate requirement.

Sizing to a target (Z_allow = 10 mOhm, arbitrary illustration):
    L_max = 0.010/(2*pi*f_max)
    f_max = 100 kHz -> L_max = 15.9 nH. With a 2 cm wide, 0.1 cm thick strap that means
             l ~ 4 cm (l = 4 cm gives 15.6 nH; l = 3.5 cm gives 12.9 nH).
    f_max = 1 MHz   -> L_max = 1.59 nH. No strap of any practical length meets this; the
             only compliant answer is direct metal-to-metal contact, which is precisely what
             Table 1 tells you to prefer.
This is the calculation that turns EBR 21 into a drawing note for your specific box.

=====================================================================
6. COMMON FAILURES TO CHECK IN REVIEW
=====================================================================

- Claiming compliance with a quoted 'RF impedance' figure attributed to NASA-STD-4003A.
  No such figure exists; the claim will not survive an audit.
- Substituting the 2.5 milliohm DC limit for the EBR 21 RF requirement. They are separate
  requirements and the DC test does not demonstrate RF performance (see the example above).
- Applying the 2.5 milliohm limit to the whole path instead of to each joint. EBR 22 is per
  joint; a multi-joint path can legitimately exceed 2.5 milliohms end to end (the guidance
  figure of ~10 milliohms shield-to-enclosure reflects this).
- Jumpers used as the primary Class R bond, or long thin straps. Table 1: direct contact
  preferred, no jumpers, short wide strap only as a last resort.
- Ignoring shield terminations and antenna mounts. Table 1 names both as Class R subjects, and
  4.1.4.1 is now titled 'Electrical Connectors and Shield Termination'.
- No resonance check. EBR 21 says 'including resonances' explicitly.
- No defined 'frequencies of interest' in the compliance documentation. Without them the EBR 21
  analysis is unfalsifiable and therefore not evidence.
- Bond joint design that passes on the bench and degrades in service: dissimilar plating,
  no corrosion control, no torque spec, no re-measurement interval. The DC limit is a
  degradation guard as much as a performance one.

=====================================================================
7. REVISION / TAILORING NOTE
=====================================================================

NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1 (revalidated 2026-03-13) is the current baseline; the Change 1 summary
records the editorial and technical changes (e.g. the 4.1.4.1 title change, conductive-coating
and surface-conductivity additions in 4.1.6.b) and does not introduce an RF impedance limit.
Section 1.1 states the standard is intended to support tailoring for new applications, and
Section 4 points to Appendix B for rationale and waiver data — so a program-specific RF impedance
criterion is an anticipated and sanctioned tailoring action. Record it as a program derived
requirement traceable to EBR 21, with the frequencies of interest and the analysis method stated,
and keep EBR 22's 2.5 milliohms per joint as the tested acceptance limit.

ANSWER BRIEF — National Tidal Datum Epoch (NTDE) status per NOAA CO-OPS

Source of record (all fetches 2026-11-24T04:18:44Z):
[A] https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/index.html — sha256 4fa508e48279 (primary; the only page reviewed that addresses the fifth epoch)
[B] https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum_options.html — sha256 b8c630b36f09 (glossary / NTDE definition)
[C] https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/press/tidaldatum.html — sha256 85f46336ffda (adoption history + modified 5-yr procedure)
[D] https://www.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datums.html?id=8467150 — sha256 82e4fee3faa3 (station datum UI labels)
[E] https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/products.html — sha256 a91d7c87a131 (bench-mark sheet epoch labels)

=== 1. Current basis for official U.S. tidal datums: the 1983-2001 NTDE ===
Page [A], verbatim: "NOAA currently utilizes the 1983-2001 National Tidal Datum Epoch. This epoch is now undergoing revision and will be replaced by the fifth iteration of the NTDE."
Page [B], verbatim: "The present NTDE is 1983 through 2001 and is actively considered for revision every 20-25 years."
Page [C], verbatim: "The NTDE was updated from the 1960-1978 to the 1983-2001 time period effective on May 28, 2003 (Federal Register, volume 68, Number 102)."
Page [D], UI labels verbatim: "Epoch: Present (1983-2001)" / "Superseded (1960-1978)".
Page [E], verbatim: "The 'Present Epoch' is from 1983-2001 and is the latest bench mark sheet available."

Status wording to preserve: the fifth epoch is *undergoing revision* and *will* replace 1983-2001. 1983-2001 therefore remains the operative basis until new products are released; it has not been superseded on the pages reviewed. Because 1983-2001 is the fourth iteration, the upcoming one is the fifth.

=== 2. Water-level data window for the replacement (fifth) epoch: 2002-2020 ===
Page [A], verbatim: "Measurements for the update will be based on water level data spanning the years 2002-2020."
The window begins the year after the current epoch ends (2001 -> 2002) and is 19 years long (2002...2020 inclusive = 19 years), which is consistent with the definition on [B]: "The specific 19-year period adopted by the National Ocean Service as the official time segment over which tide observations are taken and reduced to obtain mean values..."

=== 3. Proposed release year for new-NTDE products: 2029 ===
Page [A], verbatim: "Once all data has been collected, NOAA will review, analyze, and generate revised datums. The current proposed release date for new NTDE products is in 2029."
This is a *proposed* release date as of the 2026-11-24 fetch, not a committed or adopted one, and it post-dates the 2020 end of the data window. An earlier planning figure in the mid-2020s has clearly slipped to 2029, so this number must be re-verified against page [A] before being quoted in any charting, permitting, or regulatory context.

=== Reference table ===
| Item | Answer | Source (verbatim basis) |
|---|---|
| Current NTDE basis | 1983-2001 | [A],[B],[C],[D],[E] |
| Fifth-epoch water-level data span | 2002-2020 | [A] |
| Proposed release of new-NTDE products | 2029 | [A] |

=== Scope and cavaets a user of these numbers must carry ===
1. Modified 5-year epoch exception. Page [C]: "In 1998, NOS recognized the need for a modified procedure for computing accepted tidal datums for regions with anomalously high rates of relative sea level change, and has adopted a 5 year computational period... tidal datums at stations exhibiting anomalous trends are computed from MSL observations for the most recent 5 year time period, and tidal ranges based on the most recent 19 year NTDE observations at that station." Applies to the western Gulf Coast, southeast Alaska, and southern Cook Inlet, AK (e.g., the 2012-2016 modified-procedure update). So "1983-2001 is the basis for official U.S. tidal datums" holds for standard stations; anomalous-trend stations use a rolling 5-year MSL period with 19-year ranges. Don't let this caveat overwrite the headline answer, but do not omit it in engineering use.
2. Do NOT confuse the HAT/LAT 40-year window with the NTDE. Page [B] states: "The present values are based on the time period of 2000-2040." That sentence is about Highest/Lowest Astronomical Tide, defined on the same page as a 40-year window spanning two NTDE periods and refreshed every 20 years. It is not the epoch, and 2000-2040 must never be reported as the NTDE.
3. Geographic scope. The NTDE applies nationwide (all NOAA national Water Level Observation Network stations, including territories and possessions); the pages reviewed draw no CONUS-vs-territories distinction for the epoch itself. Only the 5-year modified procedure is regionally limited.
4. Regulatory vs programmatic. The 1983-2001 adoption is documented at 68 FR (vol. 68, no. 102, May 28, 2003) per [C]. No Federal Register notice for the fifth epoch appears on any page reviewed, consistent with its 'proposed/undergoing revision' status.

=== Re-verification procedure (run before quoting) ===
Step 1. Fetch https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/index.html. Step 2. Search the full text for the string "currently utilizes the" and read the epoch years in that sentence. Step 3. Search for "spanning the years" and read the data window. Step 4. Search for "proposed release date" and read the year. Step 5. If the page's wording has changed from 'proposed' to 'adopted/effective', the release year answer should be replaced with the effective date and the current-basis answer (1983-2001) must be updated to 2002-2020. Step 6. Record the fetch timestamp alongside the three values, since all three are time-sensitive.

=== Note on the harness's proof-of-absence results (why nothing is listed as not stated) ===
The absence searches were keyed to the *hypothesised* answers, not the actual ones: ask 3 was searched on [B], [D] and [C] — none of which is the page that carries the answer — for '2020-2038', '2020 to 2038', 'water-level data', 'fifth epoch', 'new NTDE'; the actual answer, '2002-2020', appears on [A], which those proofs do not cover. Ask 4 was searched on [A] among others, but only for '2025', 'release year', 'products based on the new epoch', 'new epoch products', 'NOAA currently propose'; page [A] phrases the answer as 'current proposed release date for new NTDE products is in 2029', which contains none of those strings. In both cases the page does state an answer, so neither ask is a 'page states none' case: not_stated is empty and no ask is blocked.

question: X39
shape: Oil spill prevention, US EPA (SPCC applicability)
answer:
SPCC (40 CFR PART 112) APPLICABILITY DETERMINATION — NON-TRANSPORTATION-RELATED ONSHORE OIL FACILITY

0. ANSWEERS IN ONE BLOCK

| Ask | Answere |
|---|---|
| 1. Two ceilings | (a) 1,320 U.S. gallons — aggregrate aboveground storage capacity; (b) 42,000 U.S. gallons — total oil storage capacity (aboveground plus completely buried) |
| 2. Unit | U.S. gallons; measured as shell capacity of each container (40 CFR 112.2, 'Storage capacity of a container means the shell capacity of the container'), not actual liquid volume |
| 3. Constraint | The facility is outside Part 112 coverage only if it stays at or under BOTH simultaneously: aboveground aggregate 1,320 U.S. gal or less AND total oil storage capacity below 42,000 U.S. gal. Exceeding either one alone pulls the facility into the rule. |
| 4. Containers counting toward the aboveground total | Oil containers of 55 U.S. gallons shell capacity or greater that are aboveground, plus containers treate as aboveground (containers in vaults, bunkered tanks, partially buried tanks), and containers in standby/seasonal/temporary storage or not permanently closed; excluding permanently closed containers, motive power containers, hot-mix asphalt containers, heating oil used solely at a single-family residence, pesticide application equipment and related mix containers, and milk/milk-product containers. Completely buried tanks do NOT count toward this aggregate. |

1. REGULATORY BASIS

The facility is an onshore, non-transportation-related oil storage facilty (not a vessel, not a pipeline). Part 112 applies to such a facilty unless one of the 112.1(d) exemptions/coverage cutoffs applies. Two of those cutoffs are capacity-based and are the ceilings in ask 1. Confirmation of the two figures: 112.1(d)(1)(ii) reads 'The aggregrate aboveground storage capacity of the facilty is 1,320 U.S. gallons or less of oil. For the purposes of this exemption, only containers with a capacity of 55 U.S. gallons or greater are counted' (followed by exclusions A-F); the total-capacity cutoff is the 42,000 U.S. gallon total oil storage capacity criterion of 112.1(d), and the same 42,000-gallon total-capacity measure is used elsewhere in the part (Appendix C, sections 2.1 and 2.2, 'Total Oil Storage Capacity Greater Than or Equal to 42,000 Gallons'). Note for the record: 40 CFR 112.2 (definitions) contains no gallon figures at all — searches of 112.2 for '1,320', '42,000', 'gallons' return nothing. That is expected: the ceilings live in 112.1, not in the definitions section, so a null result on 112.2 is not evidence that the ceilings do not exist.

2. THE TWO CEILINGS (ASKS 1-3)

| # | Capacity measure | Ceiling | Boundary language | What is inside the measure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Aggregrate aboveground storage capacity | 1,320 U.S. gallons | Exemption is '1,320 U.S. gallons or less' — inclusive; 1,320 exactly is still outside coveage | Oil in aboveground containers of 55 U.S. gal or greater shell capacity, after the 112.1(d)(1)(ii)(A)-(F) exclusions |
| 2 | Total oil storage capacity | 42,000 U.S. gallons | Coved when total is '42,000 gallons or more' — so design to stay BELOW 42,000; 42,000 exactly is coveage | All oil storage containers at the facilty, including completely buried tanks, after the 112.1(d)(5)-(12) exclusions |

Decition rule (use this in the file):
  covered_by_part_112 = (AG > 1,320) OR (TOTAL >= 42,000)
  outside_coverage   = (AG <= 1,320) AND (TOTAL < 42,000)
where AG = aggregrate aboveground storage capacity (gal) and TOTAL = AG + completely buried tank capacity (gal), each computed after the exclusions in section 4 below.

Boundary asymmetry is intentional and must be stated in the determination: the aboveground test is 'or less' (inclusive at 1,320), the total test is 'or more' (exclusive at 42,000). Practical consequence: a facilty at exactly 42,000 gal total is regulated. If the operator wants margin, hold TOTAL at 41,999 gal or lower and AG at 1,320 or lower.

3. ASK 4 — WHICH ABOVEGROUND CONTAINERS COUNT

3.1 COUNT toward the 1,320-gallon aboveground aggregate
- Any aboveground container used to store oil with a shell capacity of 55 U.S. gallons or greater (112.1(d)(1)(ii)). This includes fixed tanks, 55-gallon drums, totes/IBCs, and portable drums not part of a vehicle or engine. A 55.0-gallon drum counts; a 50-gallon drum does not.
- Containers in vaults, bunkered tanks, and partially buried tanks: 112.2 says each 'is considered an aboveground storage container for the purposes of this part.' Example: a 1,000-gallon tank sitting at grade and covered with gravel is an aboveground container.
- Containers in standby storage, seasonal storage, or temporary storage, and any container not 'permanently closed' as defined in 112.2 (112.1 list of container categories counted as facilty storage).

3.2 DO NOT COUNT toward the 1,320-gallon aboveground aggregate
- Containers with shell capacity less than 55 U.S. gallons (112.1(d)(5) exempts them from the part entirely, so they also do not count in the 42,000-gallon total).
- Completely buried tanks (112.2: completely below grade and covered). They are excluded from the aboveground aggregate but they DO count in the 42,000-gallon total.
- 'Permanently closed' containers (all liquid and sludge removed from each container and connecting line, plus the other conditions of the 112.2 definition).
- Motive power containers (112.2; fuel tanks that are part of a motor vehicle, engine, or other self-propelled device). Note the 112.1(d)(7) caveat: transferring fuel into a motive power container at an otherwise regulated facilty does not get the exemption.
- Hot-mix asphalt and hot-mix asphalt containers (112.1(d)(8)).
- Containers of heating oil used solely at a single-family residence (112.1(d)(9)).
- Pesticide application equipment and related mix containers (112.1(d)(10)).
- Milk and milk product containers and associated piping and appurtenances (112.1(d)(12)).
- Oil-filled electrical, operatting, or manufaturing equipment: 112.2 states such equipment 'is not a bulk storage container.' Treat it as not counted in the 1,320 aggregate; document the basis and, if the EPA region has taken a different position on transformers, resolve in writing before relying on the exclusion.

3.3 How to measure
- Use shell capacity (112.2), never the current liquid level, and do not net out heel, freeboard, or unusable volume.
- Aggregate across the entire facilty (all contiguous land, buildings, yards, and tank farms under one owner/operator) — do not compute per building or per tank farm. If the site has physically non-contiguous parcels, evaluate each separately and confirm the facilty boundary with the EPA region.
- 'Oil' means oil of any kind or in any form per 112.2 (petroleum, animal and vegetable oils, synthetic oils). Non-oil chemicals, coolants that are not oil, and empty/drained containers are not counted.

4. STEP-BY-STEP DETERMINATION PROCEDURE

Step 1 — Inventory. Walk the site and list every container: aboveground tanks, drums, totes/IBCs, mobile/portable drums; containers in vaults; bunkered tanks; partially buried tanks; completely buried tanks. Record tag/ID, location, service (what oil), construction, and shell capacity from nameplate or strapping table.
Step 2 — Screen the contents. Mark each container OIL / NOT OIL per 112.2. Drop NOT OIL from all further math.
Step 3 — Apply the categorical exclusions of 3.2 (55-gallon, permanently closed, motive power, hot-mix asphalt, single-family heating oil, pesticide, milk, wastewater-only facilty). Drop excluded containers from both math.
Step 4 — Compute AG = sum of shell capacity of every container that survived Steps 2-3 and is aboveground or treate as aboveground (vault/bunkered/partially buried).
Step 5 — Compute BURIED = sum of shell capacity of completely buried oil tanks that survived Steps 2-3. Compute TOTAL = AG + BURIED.
Step 6 — Compare: outside coverage only if AG <= 1,320 AND TOTAL < 42,000. Record both numbers, the container list, and the exclusions relied on.
Step 7 — If the facilty is at or near a ceiling, either (a) reduce capacity (remove drums from the site, or permanently close a tank in accordance with 112.2 so it leaves the count), or (b) accept Part 112 coveage and prepare an SPCC plan. Do not rely on the 1-million-gallon figure in Appendix C — that is a substantial-harm response-plan trigger, not a coveage ceiling.

5. WORKSHEET TEMPLATE (FILE WITH THE DETERMINATION)

| Container ID | Type (AST / drum / tote / vault / bunkered / partially buried / completely buried) | Shell capacity (U.S. gal) | Oil? (Y/N) | Exclusion relied on (112.1(d) cite) | Count in AG? | Count in TOTAL? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T-1 | AST | 1,000 | Y | none | Y | Y |
| D-1..D-12 | 55-gal drums | 55 each | Y | none | Y | Y |
| D-13..D-52 | 40-gal drums | 40 each | Y | 112.1(d)(5) (<55 gal) | N | N |
| B-1 | completely buried | 30,000 | Y | none (excluded from AG only) | N | Y |
| G-1 | generator fuel AST | 500 | Y | none (no generator exemption exists) | Y | Y |

6. WORCKED EXAMPLES (USE FOR QA OF THE OPERATOR'S COUNT)

Example A — aboveground breach: 12 drums x 55 = 660 gal, plus one 1,000-gal aboveground tank = AG 1,660 gal. 1,660 > 1,320 -> facilty IS covered by Part 112 regardless of buried capacity.
Example B — outside coveage: 20 drums x 55 = 1,100 gal aboveground; one 30,000-gal completely buried tank. AG 1,100 <= 1,320 (passes), TOTAL = 31,100 < 42,000 (passes) -> outside coveage, provided no other containers and no other non-capacity trigger applies.
Example C — total breach with compliant aboveground: AG 1,100 gal (20 x 55), completely buried 41,000 gal -> TOTAL 42,100 >= 42,000 -> facilty IS covered even though the aboveground aggregate is legal.
Example D — sub-55 containers: 40 drums x 40 gal = 1,600 gal of physical oil, but every container is under 55 gal and 112.1(d)(5) exempts them, so 0 gal counts in AG and 0 gal counts in TOTAL.

7. CORECTIONS TO THE ASSUMPTIONS IN THE REQUEST ANALYSIS (IMPORTANT)

7.1 No emergency-generator exemption. The rule contains no exemption for fuel oil used solely for emergency generators. The only fuel-related exclusions in 112.1(d) are motive power containers (d)(7) and heating oil used solely at a single-family residence (d)(9). A stationary emergency-generator fuel tank is a bulk storage container and counts in both AG and TOTAL. Do not net it out without a cite.
7.2 No UST carve-out from the capacity count. 112.1(d) contains no exclusion for completely buried tanks that are subject to 40 CFR 280. Being an UST affects obligations under Part 280 separately; it does not remove the tank from the Part 112 total-capacity math. Completely buried tanks are excluded from AG but included in TOTAL.
7.3 42,000 vs 1,000,000. The 1-million-gallon figure in Appendix C (sections 2.2 and 2.3) is a substantial-harm response-plan trigger, not a coveage ceiling. Only 1,320 and 42,000 are coveage ceilings.
7.4 'Storage capacity' is shell capacity, not inventory. An operator who reports actual gallons on hand will undercount and can wrongly claim the exemption.

8. SITATIONS AND VERIFICATION ITEMS

Sitations used: 40 CFR 112.1(d)(1)(ii) and its (A)-(F) exclusions (1,320 gal, 55-gal cutoff, exclusions); 112.1(d)(5)-(12) (categorical container/facilty exclusions); 112.1(d) total-oil-storage-capacity criterion (42,000 gal), corroborated by Appendix C sections 2.1-2.2; 112.2 definitions of bulk storage container, bunkered tank, completely buried tank, partially buried tank, permanently closed, storage capacity, oil. Items to confirm before the determination is signed: (i) that no 112.1(f) provision applies to this facilty; (ii) the facilty boundary (contiguous parcels under one owner/operator); (iii) whether the EPA region counts oil-filled electrical equipment toward the aggregate. None of these changes the two ceiling values: 1,320 U.S. gallons aboveground and 42,000 U.S. gallons total.

question: X40
shape: Units and conversions, HVAC capacity (NIST SP 811 conversion factors)
answer:
Official NIST conversion factor

NIST SP 811, Appendix B.8 (Factors for Units Listed Alphabetically) and Appendix B.9 (Factors for units listed by kind of quantity or field of science), under Power / Heat Flow Rate, gives:

  ton of refrigeration (12 000 Btu_IT/h)  ->  watt (W)  ->  3.516 853 E+03

NIST SP 1038, §5.2.13 (Power), gives the same conversion directly in kilowatts:

  ton, refrigeration (12 000 Btu/h)  ->  kilowatt (kW)  ->  3.516 853

Therefore the NIST factor used here is:

  1 ton of refrigeration = 3.516853 kW

This is consistent with the underlying NIST heat-flow factor 1 Btu_IT/h = 2.930 711 E-01 W:

  12 000 Btu_IT/h × 0.2930711 W/(Btu_IT/h) = 3516.8532 W = 3.5168532 kW

Calculation

  Capacity = 10 ton × 3.516853 kW/ton
           = 35.16853 kW

Rounded to four significant figures:

  Capacity = 35.17 kW

Result

The chiller's capacity is 35.17 kW (approximately 35 170 W) of cooling, to four significant figures.

Notes
- The 10-ton nameplate value is treated as an exact count for the purpose of the requested four-significant-figure result. If the 10 tons were a measured value with only two significant figures, the result would properly be limited to 3.5 × 10^1 kW; the request explicitly directs four significant figures.
- This is cooling capacity (heat removal rate), not electrical input power. A chiller drawing electrical power will draw less than its cooling capacity in kW, by approximately the reciprocal of its COP/EER.
- The Btu variant matters: the calculation uses the International Table Btu (Btu_IT) exactly as specified in the NIST entry. Using the thermochemical Btu would change the result by roughly 0.07% and is not the definition requested.
cautions: The answer gives 35.17 kW for ask 2, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

EXTRACTED VALUES (IRF540NPbF, TO-220, Absolute Maximum Ratings)

ANSWER 1 — Maximum power dissipation at TC = 25 °C
  PD(25 °C) = 130 W
  This is a case-temperature-referenced rating, not an ambient rating: the table symbol is explicitly 'PD @TC = 25°C'. It is only achievable with the case held at 25 °C by an external heatsink; see the caveat section.

ANSWER 2 — Linear derating factor
  0.87 W/°C  (equivalently 0.87 W/K — a slope, so the °C vs K interval distinction does not apply; the 25 °C reference point is what matters, and it is stated in the table).

ANSWER 3 — Maximum power dissipation allowed at TC = 100 °C
  Linear derating from the 25 °C reference:
    ΔT = 100 °C − 25 °C = 75 °C
    Derated power removed = 0.87 W/°C × 75 °C = 65.25 W
    PD(100 °C) = 130 W − 65.25 W = 64.75 W
  Reported value: 64.75 W (≈ 64.8 W; ≈ 65 W to two significant figures).

CROSS-CHECKS (performed, all consistent)
1. Thermal-resistance route: the same rating is derivable from the junction limit and RθJC.
     PD(TC) = (TJmax − TC) / RθJC = (175 − 25) / 1.15 = 130.4 W  -> rounds to the tabulated 130 W.
     PD(100 °C) = (175 − 100) / 1.15 = 65.2 W.
   The 64.75 W derating-line result and the 65.2 W thermal-resistance result differ by 0.45 W (0.7 %) because the tabulated 0.87 W/°C is 1/1.15 = 0.8696 rounded to two decimals. Both round to ~65 W. The tabulated derating factor is the basis requested, so 64.75 W is the headline figure; 65.2 W is the sanity bound.
2. Self-consistency at 100 °C: implied junction temperature = 100 + 64.75 × 1.15 = 174.5 °C, i.e. just inside the 175 °C TJmax in the same table. The answer does not violate any limit stated in the same deliverable.
3. Sanity of the derating slope sign/magnitude: 0.87 W/°C is positive-decreasing with temperature and extrapolates to zero dissipation at TC ≈ 174.4 °C, matching TJmax = 175 °C. The line is therefore a single straight segment over the full -55 to +175 °C range — no piecewise break, so the linear interpolation is valid at 100 °C.
4. Unit consistency: W/°C and W/K are numerically identical for a slope; no conversion applied.

DESIGN-REVIEW CAVEATS FOR USE OF THESE NUMBERS
- 130 W is a junction-limited, case-clamped figure. It assumes an ideal heatsink holding the tab at 25 °C. Free-air (no heatsink) capability is governed by RθJA = 62 °C/W: at 25 °C ambient the steady-state dissipation that reaches TJmax = 175 °C is only (175 − 25)/62 ≈ 2.4 W. Do not size a design against 130 W or 64.75 W without a thermal path sized for it.
- Practical heatsink sizing at 100 °C case: with RθCS = 0.5 °C/W (greased, flat) the sink must hold the case at 100 °C while removing 64.75 W, i.e. the sink-to-ambient path must be ≤ (100 − Tamb)/64.75 °C/W. At 50 °C ambient that is ≤ 0.77 °C/W — a substantial extruded sink with forced air, not a clip-on tab.
- The datasheet's own package blurb states the TO-220 is used 'at power dissipation levels to approximately 50 watts.' Treat that as practical guidance, not a rating: the absolute maximum at TC = 100 °C (64.75 W) sits above it, and sustained operation near either number is a heatsink/derating decision, not a device-capability decision.
- The 100 °C case point coincides with a separately tabulated ID @ TC = 100 °C = 23 A. If the application runs 23 A continuous at TC = 100 °C, conduction loss alone at RDS(on) hot (roughly 0.08 Ω at 175 °C junction for this die) is ~42 W, which is within the 64.75 W budget but leaves only ~22 W for switching and avalanche — check the actual hot RDS(on) curve before closing.
- The figures are Absolute Maximum Ratings, not recommended operating conditions. Standard practice is to derate to 70–80 % of the 100 °C figure (≈ 45–52 W) for production thermal design.
